prompt: You receive an email from 'hr-payroll@yourcompany-secure.net' asking you to log in to a linked portal and confirm your bank account details for the upcoming payroll run. The email looks exactly like official HR communications. What should you do immediately?
options: Click the link and update your bank details since payroll is due soon
Forward the email to a colleague to ask if they got it too
Do not click anything â€” report the email to IT Security and verify through the official HR portal
Reply to the sender asking them to confirm their identity
explanation: The domain 'yourcompany-secure.net' is not your company's real domain. Never click links in unsolicited emails asking for sensitive details. Report it to IT Security and use the official HR portal directly to check for any legitimate requests.

prompt: You step away from your desk for a 20-minute coffee break without locking your computer. A colleague notices your email inbox and shared drive are fully visible on screen. What did you do wrong?
options: You took too long a break
You left your workstation unlocked, exposing company data to anyone passing by
You forgot to close your email tab before leaving
You did not save your work before stepping away
explanation: Leaving a workstation unlocked even briefly allows anyone nearby to read, copy, or tamper with your data. Always lock your screen before walking away.

prompt: A vendor you work with regularly sends an email saying their banking details have changed and asks you to update them in the system before processing this month's invoice. What is your immediate next step?
options: Update the bank details right away so the payment is not delayed
Reply to the email confirming you have received the request
Call the vendor on their known, previously verified phone number to confirm the change before updating anything
Forward the email to your manager for approval, then update the details
explanation: Fraudulent bank-detail change requests are one of the most common ways companies lose money. Always call the vendor using a number you already have on file, never use contact details provided in the suspicious email itself.

prompt: You are working late alone in the office. A man in a delivery uniform approaches the secured door and says he has a package for reception. He asks if you can just hold the door open for him. What should you do?
options: Hold the door open â€” he is clearly a delivery person
Direct him to the intercom or reception and do not allow him through without proper access
Ask his name and let him in if it sounds legitimate
Let him in but escort him to reception yourself
explanation: Allowing someone to enter a secure area without proper verification, even if they appear legitimate, is a serious security lapse. Direct the person to the proper entry point and let the front desk or security handle it.

prompt: You receive a chat message from someone claiming to be the IT helpdesk asking for your network password so they can reset your profile remotely. What should you do?
options: Provide the password since IT staff need it to help you
Give only your username, not your password
Refuse to share your password and verify the request by calling the IT helpdesk directly on their official number
Change your password first, then share the new one
explanation: Legitimate IT helpdesks never need your password. Sharing your credentials gives anyone who asks complete access to your account. Always verify through official channels before acting.

prompt: An email lands in your inbox with the subject 'Your account will be suspended in 24 hours.' It contains a button labelled Verify Now. The sender address looks official but slightly different from usual. What should you do first?
options: Click Verify Now immediately to avoid being locked out
Hover over the link to check the real URL, then report the email to IT Security without clicking
Forward it to your manager so they can decide
Delete the email and ignore it
explanation: Urgency is a common pressure tactic. Hover to inspect the link's true destination, and report the email to IT Security. Deleting without reporting means the threat is unaddressed for others.

prompt: You find a USB drive in the office car park with a label that reads 'Q3 Salary Review â€” Confidential.' What should you do?
options: Plug it into your computer to find out who it belongs to
Hand it directly to IT Security without plugging it in anywhere
Leave it where you found it in case the owner comes back
Give it to reception to place in lost and found
explanation: Unknown USB drives can contain software that automatically runs when plugged in. Never insert them into any company device. Hand the drive to IT Security so it can be safely inspected.

prompt: Your company's finance team receives an email that appears to come from the CEO asking for an urgent wire transfer of $15,000 to a new supplier. The CEO is listed as travelling and unavailable. What should the finance officer do?
options: Process the transfer since it came from the CEO's email address
Process it but send the CEO a follow-up email for records
Pause the request and call the CEO or their PA using a known office number to verify before transferring any funds
Transfer half now and wait for further confirmation
explanation: Fraudulent payment requests impersonating executives are extremely common. No matter how urgent or how senior the apparent sender is, always verify large or unusual financial transactions through a separate, trusted communication channel.

prompt: A colleague asks to borrow your access badge just for today because she forgot hers at home. What should you do?
options: Lend her your badge since she is a trusted colleague
Accompany her everywhere she needs to go while she uses your badge
Decline and direct her to the security desk to arrange temporary access
Let her borrow it but ask for it back by lunchtime
explanation: Access badges are individually assigned and sharing them is a policy violation. If something goes wrong while someone else is using your badge, the incident is attributed to you. The security desk can issue proper temporary access.

prompt: You receive an email from 'support@microsoft-helpdesk.org' informing you that your Microsoft 365 licence has expired and you must re-enter your login credentials on their site within two hours. What should you do?
options: Click the link and re-enter your credentials before the deadline
Call Microsoft support using the number provided in the email
Do not click the link. Report the email to IT Security and check your Microsoft 365 status through the official company portal
Forward the email to IT and continue working normally
explanation: Microsoft does not use domains like 'microsoft-helpdesk.org.' This is a credential-harvesting attempt. Always report such emails and verify software status through your company's official internal portals.

prompt: You are printing a confidential HR performance review and forget to collect it from the printer for two hours. When you return, several sheets are missing. What did you do wrong?
options: You used the wrong printer settings
You printed a document that should not have been printed
You left sensitive printed documents unattended at a shared printer, creating a data exposure risk
You did not save a digital copy before printing
explanation: Shared printers are accessible to all nearby staff. Leaving sensitive documents unattended is a data handling violation. Always collect prints immediately or use secure-print features that require you to authenticate at the printer.

prompt: Someone calls you claiming to be from your company's IT department and says your computer has sent alerts suggesting a virus infection. They ask you to download a remote access tool so they can fix it. What should you do?
options: Download the tool â€” IT needs access to fix the issue
Ask them to call back later when you are less busy
Hang up, do not download anything, and call the IT helpdesk back on the official number to report and verify the issue
Tell them your computer seems fine and end the call
explanation: Unsolicited calls offering to fix your computer are a common social engineering tactic. Installing remote-access tools on command can give the caller full control of your machine. Always initiate contact with IT yourself using verified numbers.

prompt: You receive an invoice from a supplier your company uses regularly, but the invoice email comes from 'billing@supp1ier-invoices.com' instead of the usual domain. The amount and formatting look correct. What should you do?
options: Pay the invoice since the amount and details match
Reply to the email to double-check before paying
Contact the supplier directly using contact details from your existing records, not from this email, to confirm whether the invoice is genuine
Forward to your manager and let them decide
explanation: A misspelled or unfamiliar sending domain is a major warning sign. Never pay or reply based on that email alone. Use contact details you already have to confirm the invoice.

prompt: While working from a coffee shop, you take a call on your laptop's microphone to discuss a client's upcoming contract terms. Several other customers are seated nearby. What did you do wrong?
options: You did not use earphones during the call
You discussed confidential client information in a public place where others could overhear
You used public Wi-Fi without a VPN
You did not mute yourself during the call
explanation: Discussing confidential business matters in public violates client confidentiality and company policy. Sensitive calls should be made in private spaces.

prompt: Your manager asks you over messaging to share the master spreadsheet containing all employee salaries so she can review it on her personal Gmail account. What should you do?
options: Send it to her Gmail since she is your manager and has authority
Send a password-protected version to her Gmail
Decline and explain that sensitive HR data must stay within approved company systems â€” suggest she access it via the internal HR platform
Ask HR to approve the share first, then send it
explanation: Sending sensitive HR data to personal email accounts bypasses company security controls and may violate data protection policies. Even if the requester is your manager, the correct channel is the secure internal system.

prompt: An unknown person in business attire is walking confidently through your open-plan office floor without a visible visitor badge. What should you do?
options: Assume they are a new hire and do nothing
Politely approach them, ask if you can help, and if they are a visitor, escort them to reception
Alert security via email once you have finished your current task
Ask a colleague near you to check who they are
explanation: Unidentified individuals in restricted areas are a physical security risk. A polite challenge is appropriate and expected. Time matters â€” do not delay by email or delegate to a colleague who may also do nothing.

prompt: You are about to leave the office for the day and realise you have left a printed client proposal on your desk. What should you do?
options: Leave it â€” your desk is in a secure building
Turn it face down so the contents are not visible
Lock it in a drawer or a secure cabinet before leaving
Take it home so you can review it tonight
explanation: Leaving sensitive documents on an unattended desk overnight violates a clean-desk policy and risks exposure to cleaning staff or others working late. Secure it in a locked drawer or filing cabinet.

prompt: You receive a text message on your work phone saying your company VPN session has expired and you must click a link to re-authenticate. What should you do?
options: Click the link and log in to restore your VPN
Forward the text to IT to check
Do not click the link. Contact IT Security directly using the official helpdesk number to report and verify
Ignore the text and see if your VPN still works
explanation: Legitimate VPN alerts do not come via text messages linking to external sites. This is a credential-harvesting attempt. Report it through official channels so IT can investigate and warn others.

prompt: A recruiter contacts you on LinkedIn and asks you to complete a skills assessment by downloading and opening an attached Word document. What should you do?
options: Open the document â€” it is just a skills test
Download it but do not enable macros if prompted
Do not open unsolicited attachments from unknown contacts. Verify the recruiter's legitimacy through official channels before engaging
Open it on your personal laptop to keep your work laptop safe
explanation: Unsolicited documents from unknown external contacts can contain malicious code. Even disabling macros may not be sufficient protection. Verify the source first; if legitimate, they will understand your caution.

prompt: You are filling in an online HR reimbursement form and notice the page URL has changed from 'https://hr.yourcompany.com' to 'http://hr.yourcompany.com.forms-portal.net'. What should you do?
options: Continue â€” the page looks the same as usual
Stop immediately, do not submit any data, close the browser, and report the URL to IT Security
Reload the page and try again
Call HR to ask why the portal has moved
explanation: The URL has changed to a completely different domain, which is not your company's site. This is a sign you may have been redirected to a fake page. Submit no data and report it to IT Security immediately.

prompt: You share your screen during a video call with an external client and forget that your email inbox is also visible in the background, showing subject lines of several internal HR emails. What did you do wrong?
options: You used the wrong screen-sharing application
You did not prepare a formal agenda for the meeting
You exposed internal HR email subject lines to an external party by not closing or hiding them before sharing your screen
You shared your screen without IT permission
explanation: Always close, minimise, or hide any confidential windows before sharing your screen with external parties. Even subject lines can reveal sensitive internal information.

prompt: Your company uses a policy that all employees must use multi-factor authentication to access business email. A colleague disables MFA on his account because he finds the extra step annoying. What did he do wrong?
options: He changed a setting without IT approval
He removed a key layer of account protection, making his account far easier for unauthorised parties to access
He violated his employment contract
He is wasting IT resources
explanation: MFA is a critical security control that makes it significantly harder for attackers to access an account even if they have the password. Disabling it removes that protection and puts company data at serious risk.

prompt: You notice a colleague has written her network login password on a sticky note attached to her monitor. What should you do?
options: Ignore it â€” it is her business
Take a photo of it in case you ever need access to her account
Politely let her know this is a security risk and encourage her to remove it and use a password manager instead
Report her to management immediately
explanation: Passwords written in plain sight can be seen by anyone passing by, including visitors. A friendly reminder is appropriate and constructive. Password managers are the secure alternative.

prompt: An internal email from 'admin@company-allstaff-updates.net' is sent company-wide asking all employees to confirm their employee ID numbers and job titles via a linked form. What should you do?
options: Complete the form â€” it is sent to everyone so it must be official
Complete only part of the form to limit your exposure
Do not fill in the form. Verify with IT or HR through official channels whether the request is legitimate before providing any information
Reply to the email asking for confirmation that it is genuine
explanation: The domain 'company-allstaff-updates.net' is not an official company domain. Mass internal-looking emails sent from external domains are a common way to harvest employee data. Verify independently before responding.

prompt: A contractor who finished a project last month still has an active company email account and continues to receive internal communications. What should have happened when the contract ended?
options: The contractor should have asked to keep the account for reference
The account should have been deactivated by IT on or before the contractor's last day
The account is fine to keep active for three months in case questions arise
The contractor's manager should have changed the account password
explanation: Access permissions must be revoked promptly when someone leaves. Keeping accounts active creates an unnecessary risk â€” former contractors should not retain access to internal systems or communications after their engagement ends.

prompt: You are on-boarding a new employee and need to create their system account. A colleague suggests reusing a recently departed employee's account rather than creating a new one to save time. What should you do?
options: Reuse the account â€” it already has the right permissions set up
Reuse it but change the username and password first
Decline and create a fresh, properly provisioned account for the new employee
Ask IT if reusing is allowed before deciding
explanation: Reusing accounts bypasses proper access provisioning, may grant inappropriate permissions inherited from the previous user, and creates audit trail problems. Every employee should have a freshly created, correctly configured account.

prompt: You are granted temporary administrator access to a company system to complete a specific project. Once the project is done, you keep the access in case you need it later. What did you do wrong?
options: You should have asked for permanent access from the start
You retained elevated access beyond its intended purpose, which violates the principle of minimum necessary access
You did not document your use of the administrator account
You should have shared the access with your team
explanation: Access should be granted only for as long as it is needed. Retaining elevated permissions after a project ends increases risk â€” if your account is compromised, an attacker inherits those excess privileges.

prompt: Your HR department emails staff asking them to click a survey link to rate their benefits satisfaction. You hover over the link and see it leads to 'hr-survey-forms.yourcompany.com.outsidehost.biz.' What should you do?
options: Complete the survey â€” HR sent it
Skip the survey this year
Do not click the link. The domain is not your company's. Report the email to IT Security and notify HR directly so they can clarify
Forward the email to IT asking if it is safe
explanation: The link uses your company name as a subdomain on a completely different domain, which is a spoofing technique. Report it to IT and inform HR so they can send a corrected, verified communication.

prompt: A member of the administration team receives a call from someone claiming to be a government auditor who needs immediate access to payroll records. The caller says the request is urgent and bypassing normal procedures is necessary. What should the admin team member do?
options: Provide the records since it is a government request
Provide summary information only
Do not provide anything. Tell the caller that all official requests must go through the company's legal or compliance team, then report the call internally
Ask the caller to email a formal request and then process it
explanation: Legitimate auditors follow formal procedures and do not pressure staff to bypass controls urgently by phone. Impersonating an authority figure to rush you into acting is a social engineering tactic. Escalate through proper internal channels.

prompt: You notice that one of your company's shared email inboxes used by the admin team has not had its password changed in over two years, even though three people who had access have since left the company. What is the problem here?
options: The inbox should be deleted since those employees are gone
The former employees may still be able to access the shared inbox because the password was never changed after they left
The inbox should have been transferred to a new owner
Shared inboxes do not need password changes since they are monitored by the team
explanation: When people with access to a shared account leave, the password must be changed immediately. Otherwise, former employees retain potential access to company communications, which is a significant security and compliance risk.

prompt: You receive a calendar invite from an external address for a meeting titled Q4 Budget Strategy. Accepting the invite automatically grants the external sender access to view your calendar availability. What should you have considered before accepting?
options: Whether the meeting room was available
Whether accepting reveals your schedule and availability to an unknown external party
Whether your manager approved the external meeting
Whether the meeting time conflicts with team standup
explanation: Accepting calendar invites from unknown external senders can expose your schedule, including meeting titles, attendees, and availability patterns, to parties who should not have that information. Always verify the sender before accepting.

prompt: You receive an email informing you that you have won a gift card from your company's Employee of the Month programme. You do not recall entering any such programme. The email asks you to claim your prize via a link. What should you do?
options: Click the link â€” it sounds like a genuine company reward
Click the link but only enter your email address, not your password
Do not click the link. Verify with HR or your manager through known contact details whether the programme and prize are genuine
Forward the email to a colleague to see if they got it too
explanation: Unexpected prize or reward emails are a classic lure. Before clicking anything, confirm directly with HR using an official channel. If the reward is real, they can guide you through the legitimate claim process.

prompt: While reviewing the monthly expense report, a finance officer notices an invoice from a vendor that was submitted twice â€” once with the company's usual bank details and once with different account details. What should the finance officer do immediately?
options: Pay the most recent submission since it is likely an update
Pay neither and investigate both submissions, contacting the vendor through verified contact details to confirm which is legitimate
Pay both and request a refund on the duplicate
Send an email to the vendor's address in the invoice asking for clarification
explanation: Duplicate invoices with different bank details are a major red flag for payment fraud. Do not pay either until the vendor's identity and correct banking details have been confirmed using your existing, independently verified contact information.

prompt: You are asked to dispose of a stack of printed documents containing past employee performance reviews. You put them in the regular recycling bin near your desk. What did you do wrong?
options: You should have scanned them first
You disposed of sensitive HR documents in an unsecured recycling bin instead of shredding them
You should have archived them for seven years before disposing
You should have asked a manager to sign off on the disposal
explanation: Sensitive documents must be destroyed properly â€” using a cross-cut shredder or a confidential waste bin provided by a certified disposal service. Ordinary recycling bins leave documents readable and accessible.

prompt: You are working at the reception desk when a smartly dressed woman says she has an appointment with the Head of Finance but the Head has not yet arrived. She asks to wait in the finance department's open office. What should you do?
options: Show her to the finance office â€” she says she has an appointment
Ask her to wait in the designated visitor area in reception until the Head of Finance comes to collect her personally
Call the Head of Finance to confirm, and if no answer let her wait in the office
Issue her a visitor pass and let her find her own way
explanation: Visitors should never be left unaccompanied in restricted or sensitive areas. Always have them wait in the reception or visitor area until the appropriate employee personally comes to escort them.

prompt: You get an email from an address that looks like your company's domain, but the display name reads CEO Office. The email asks all department heads to send their team headcount and annual budget figures to a shared folder link by end of day. What should you do?
options: Comply â€” the display name shows it is from the CEO's office
Send the headcount but not the budget
Do not send anything. Verify the request directly with the CEO's office by phone or in person before sharing financial data
Reply to the email asking to confirm the request
explanation: Display names can be set to anything â€” they are not proof of identity. An unusual, urgent request for sensitive financial data should always be verified through a separate, trusted channel before you respond.

prompt: A new supplier registration form asks your procurement assistant to provide the company's internal finance system login credentials to verify payment capabilities. What should the procurement assistant do?
options: Provide the credentials â€” it is a standard verification step
Provide read-only credentials only
Refuse to provide any credentials. Legitimate supplier registrations never require your internal system login details. Escalate to management
Ask IT to create a guest account for the supplier
explanation: No legitimate supplier registration process requires internal system credentials. This is a strong indicator of fraud or social engineering. Report it immediately rather than attempting to accommodate the request in any form.

prompt: You are logging in to your company's HR self-service portal from home and notice your browser says Not Secure in the address bar. What should you do?
options: Log in quickly and log out as soon as you are done
Do not log in. A Not Secure warning means the connection is not encrypted. Close the page and access the portal only over a secure connection
Log in using a different browser
Clear your browser cache first, then try again
explanation: A Not Secure warning means the site is not using HTTPS, so your login credentials and data are transmitted without encryption and could be intercepted. Never enter sensitive information on an unencrypted page.

prompt: While processing payroll, you accidentally transfer the month's salary run to the wrong bank account. You realise the error within minutes. What is your immediate next step?
options: Wait to see if the recipient returns the funds
Tell your manager by email and document the error
Immediately call your bank to request a recall of the transfer, and notify your manager and the finance compliance team at the same time
Contact the recipient directly to request a refund
explanation: Misdirected payments must be escalated immediately â€” banks have limited time windows to recall transfers. Every minute counts. Notify both the bank and your internal finance compliance team without delay.

prompt: You receive a WhatsApp message from someone claiming to be your company's CFO saying she is in an important meeting and needs you to urgently buy gift vouchers and send her the codes. What should you do?
options: Buy the vouchers â€” she is the CFO and it sounds urgent
Ask the CFO to confirm via her company email first
Do not buy anything. Gift card requests via messaging apps from apparent senior figures are a known fraud. Verify by calling the CFO directly on her official office number
Buy half the amount as a compromise while you verify
explanation: Gift card fraud via impersonation of senior colleagues is extremely common and is almost always irreversible once done. Legitimate executives do not make financial requests through personal messaging apps. Call the person directly using a verified number.

prompt: You get an email from your company's finance team email address asking you to log in to a linked external website and update your payroll bank account details. What should you do?
options: Follow the link â€” it came from the finance team's official address
Log in but only update partial details and wait for confirmation
Do not click the link. Even legitimate email addresses can be compromised. Verify directly with payroll by phone and access the payroll portal using a bookmarked URL
Reply to the email saying you will update your details shortly
explanation: A genuine sending address does not guarantee a genuine email â€” accounts can be compromised. Legitimate payroll teams never ask you to enter banking details on external websites. Always verify through a separate channel.

prompt: You need to send a large spreadsheet of client financial data to an external auditor. What is the most appropriate way to do this?
options: Email it as an attachment from your work account
Upload it to your personal Google Drive and share the link
Use your company's approved secure file-transfer method and password-protect the document, then send the password separately
Print it and courier it to the auditor's office
explanation: Sensitive financial data must be transferred using approved, encrypted methods. Emailing unencrypted attachments or using personal cloud storage bypasses company controls. Password-protect the file and send credentials through a separate channel for added security.

prompt: You receive an email with the subject 'All staff must complete mandatory cyber training by Friday' containing a link to an external site. The email appears to come from HR but the sender address ends in '@hrtrainingportal.online.' What should you do?
options: Click the link and complete the training quickly before the deadline
Reply to the email confirming you will do it
Do not click the link. Verify with HR directly that the training is genuine and ask for the official link via your company's learning management system
Forward the email to IT and wait indefinitely
explanation: External domains impersonating internal departments are a common way to steal credentials under the guise of mandatory training. Always verify training communications directly with HR and access training through your company's official internal platform.

prompt: You are setting up a new password for your HR portal account and choose to use the same password you use for your personal Gmail account. What is wrong with this approach?
options: Personal passwords are usually too short for corporate systems
If your personal Gmail account is ever compromised, the same credentials could be used to access your work systems, putting company data at risk
HR portals require passwords to be created by IT
It is against company policy to use passwords with fewer than twelve characters
explanation: Reusing passwords across personal and professional accounts means a breach of one can lead to access of the other. Always use unique, strong passwords for each account, ideally managed through an approved password manager.

prompt: A finance manager is reviewing supplier contracts and notices that one supplier's address, contact name, and bank details all changed at the same time following an email received two months ago. She does not recall authorising the changes. What should she do immediately?
options: Continue paying the supplier since the changes are already in the system
Freeze all payments to that supplier and immediately escalate to senior management and the compliance team to investigate the changes
Send an email to the updated contact address asking for confirmation
Revert the details to the old ones and continue payments
explanation: Simultaneous changes to all supplier details are a strong indicator that a fraudster has redirected payments. All payments must be paused immediately while the changes are investigated through original verified contact details.

prompt: You are in the office kitchen when two colleagues start discussing specific salary figures for named employees. You are not part of the conversation. What should you consider doing?
options: Listen carefully in case the information is useful later
Join the conversation so the discussion is more controlled
Gently remind them that discussing specific salary details about named individuals in a communal area risks breaching employee confidentiality
Report them to HR immediately
explanation: Salary data is sensitive personal information. Discussing it in communal, non-private spaces risks being overheard by other staff or visitors, which can harm individuals and violate data protection principles. A polite reminder is appropriate.

prompt: You get an email from 'do-not-reply@company-system-update.com' saying your company's internal directory has been updated and you need to re-register your details via the attached Word document. What should you do?
options: Open the form and complete it
Open the form but do not enable macros
Do not open the attachment or provide any information. Report the email to IT Security and verify with your HR or admin team whether any re-registration is taking place
Complete the form but submit it by printing and handing it to HR
explanation: Unexpected emails from unofficial domains asking you to open documents and submit personal details are a common attack method. The Word document could also contain harmful code. Always verify through internal channels before opening attachments from unknown senders.

prompt: Your company has a policy requiring all employees to lock their computers before leaving their desks. You observe a colleague regularly leaving her computer unlocked when she goes to meetings. What should you do?
options: Ignore it â€” it is her risk to take
Lock her computer on her behalf each time she leaves
Remind her of the policy in a friendly way and, if it continues, raise it with your line manager or IT Security
Leave a note on her keyboard
explanation: A friendly reminder is the first step. Locking someone else's computer on their behalf is a short-term measure but does not address the behaviour. Persistent non-compliance with security policy should be escalated appropriately.

prompt: Your building's key card system goes offline temporarily and a security guard manually opens the entrance door for anyone approaching. A member of the public follows a group of employees inside. What should the nearest employee do?
options: Assume the person is with one of the other employees
Ask the person to show ID to the security guard and ensure they sign in as a visitor
Hold the next door open for them to be polite
Notify the facilities team by email once at their desk
explanation: Physical security must continue to be enforced even when automated systems are offline. Any person not clearly identified as an employee should be directed to sign in through the visitor process, regardless of the circumstances.

prompt: You are away from the office for a week and set up an out-of-office reply that includes your full name, job title, department, direct manager's name, and the name of the project you are working on. What is the risk?
options: Your manager might not like being named in the out-of-office
The project name could give external parties sensitive details about internal activities, and listing your manager gives social engineers a ready-made target to impersonate
Your out-of-office will expire before you return
External parties may reply to your manager instead of you
explanation: Out-of-office messages visible to external senders should be minimal. Sharing project names, manager names, and organisational details helps social engineers craft convincing follow-up attacks targeting you or your colleagues.

prompt: Your company's procurement team receives a phone call from someone claiming to represent a software vendor, saying your current licence is about to expire and you need to provide a purchase order number immediately to avoid service interruption. What should they do?
options: Provide the purchase order number to avoid downtime
Ask the caller to call back tomorrow
Tell the caller you will call back using the contact details on the vendor's official website, then verify the licence status independently
Raise a purchase order and send it to the email the caller provides
explanation: Unsolicited calls creating urgency around licences or services are a social engineering tactic to extract sensitive procurement information. Always verify by calling back on a number you independently look up, not one the caller provides.

prompt: An email arrives in the finance team's shared inbox appearing to be a legitimate monthly bank statement from the company's main bank. The statement shows an unexpected large debit. What should the finance team do first?
options: Log on to the bank's official website directly to verify whether the transaction appears on the real account
Reply to the email sender asking for an explanation of the debit
Call the number listed in the email to query the charge
Forward the email to the bank's customer service address from the email
explanation: Always verify unexpected transactions by logging on to the bank's official, bookmarked website directly â€” never use links, phone numbers, or email addresses contained in the email itself, which could be spoofed.

prompt: You are in a meeting where someone photographs a whiteboard covered in budgets, staffing levels, and strategic targets for next year. She says it is just for her notes. What should you consider doing?
options: Let her â€” it is just for her own use
Ask her to delete it after the meeting
Politely ask whether photographing sensitive business information on a personal device is permitted under company policy, and raise it with your manager if unsure
Notify IT Security that photos were taken in the meeting
explanation: Photographing sensitive internal information with personal devices creates a data leakage risk and may violate company policy. Raising the question is appropriate â€” the answer may depend on company rules and whether the person is an employee or visitor.

prompt: Your manager asks you to email a file of employee home addresses and emergency contact details to the company's new HR software vendor so they can set up the system. What should you do before sending?
options: Email it immediately since the manager has authorised it
Confirm the vendor's email address and send
Check that the vendor has a signed data processing agreement with your company and that the transfer is approved by your data protection officer before sending any personal data
Send only half the records first to test the connection
explanation: Transferring personal data to a third party requires a legal data processing agreement to be in place. Sending sensitive personal data without confirming this may violate data protection law, regardless of whether a manager has verbally authorised it.

prompt: You receive an email from 'notifications@linkedln.com' â€” note the letter substitution â€” telling you that someone viewed your profile and you should log in to see who. What should you do?
options: Click the login link to see who viewed your profile
Do not click the link. The domain is not LinkedIn. Report the email and visit linkedin.com directly in a new browser tab if you want to check your profile
Forward it to IT â€” they will investigate
Reply to unsubscribe
explanation: The domain uses a lowercase letter substitution designed to fool quick readers. Always examine email domains carefully and navigate to websites by typing the address directly, not via links in emails.

prompt: A delivery driver asks to use a computer at the reception desk for just a minute to check a delivery postcode. The receptionist allows it. What did the receptionist do wrong?
options: She left the delivery driver unsupervised
She allowed an unverified visitor to access a company computer, which could expose data or introduce harmful software
She should have offered her phone instead
She did not log the visitor properly
explanation: Company computers â€” even at reception â€” should never be handed over to external visitors. A brief use can be enough to access sensitive files, introduce malicious software, or note credentials. Offer to help them directly rather than handing over the device.

prompt: You notice a new colleague has been copied on sensitive finance emails that are outside her job role. When you ask, she says her manager approved it. What should you do?
options: Accept the explanation since a manager approved it
Remove her from the email thread yourself
Raise a formal query with IT Security or your data governance team to ensure the access is properly approved and documented
Ask her manager to confirm in writing before doing anything
explanation: Access to sensitive information should be granted through a formal, documented process â€” not informally via email CC. Raising it with IT Security or data governance ensures that if approval was genuine, it gets recorded, and if not, it gets addressed.

prompt: During a team call, someone shares their screen and their password manager is visible for a moment with several saved passwords partially visible. What should be done immediately?
options: Nothing â€” the passwords were only partially visible
The presenter should stop sharing, close the password manager, and change any passwords that may have been visible
The meeting participants should delete their recordings
IT Security should be notified so they can remotely wipe all attendee screens
explanation: Even a partial view of saved passwords is a security incident. The presenter should stop sharing immediately, close the application, and change any passwords that might have been seen. Any recording of the call should also be deleted or restricted.

prompt: Your company's administration team routinely uses a free consumer-grade file-sharing service to send contracts and agreements between offices because it is easier than the official system. What is the problem with this?
options: The free service is slower than the official system
Consumer cloud services do not meet corporate security, compliance, and data residency requirements for sensitive business documents
The official system has a size limit that the free service does not
IT will not be able to help if there is a problem with the free service
explanation: Consumer file-sharing services are designed for personal use and typically lack the encryption, access controls, audit trails, and compliance certifications required for business contracts. Always use the approved corporate system.

prompt: An employee in HR receives a call from someone who says they are the new IT manager and needs the employee list with home addresses to set up home-working equipment delivery. What should the HR employee do?
options: Send the list since it is an internal IT request
Ask for the IT manager's employee ID and then send the list
Tell the caller that personal employee data cannot be shared without a formal, verified request from HR leadership, and offer to call back the IT manager through the official directory
Send a partial list with names only, no addresses
explanation: Personal employee data should never be shared based on an unsolicited phone call, regardless of who the caller claims to be. Verify the person's identity through official channels before releasing any sensitive information.

prompt: You use your work laptop to connect to a hotel's public Wi-Fi during a business trip and access your company's finance system without using the VPN. What did you do wrong?
options: You should have used the hotel's wired connection instead
You connected to a company system over an unsecured public network without encryption, exposing your session and data to potential interception
You should have asked the hotel for their Wi-Fi security certificate first
You logged in outside office hours without authorisation
explanation: Public Wi-Fi networks are unsecured and can be monitored by anyone on the same network. Always connect via your company's VPN when using public Wi-Fi or any untrusted network to encrypt your traffic.

prompt: You receive an email appearing to be from a senior colleague, asking you to approve a new supplier and add them to the payment system. The email says to act before the colleague's meeting starts in ten minutes. What should you do?
options: Approve it quickly before the meeting starts
Approve it and send a confirmation email afterwards
Pause the request, verify it by calling or messaging the colleague directly using a known contact, and only proceed once genuinely confirmed
Ask the supplier to email you directly with their details before you proceed
explanation: Artificial time pressure is used to prevent careful thought. No legitimate business request should bypass verification. A quick phone call or chat message to the colleague takes seconds and protects the company from fraud.

prompt: A new employee has been given a company laptop and is using it to play online games on a gaming platform during lunch. She says she is on her personal time. What is the issue?
options: She is wasting her lunch break
Online gaming platforms can introduce software or vulnerabilities to a corporate device, and personal use of company equipment may violate acceptable-use policy
The company's internet speed may be affected
She should have used her phone for gaming instead
explanation: Company devices are subject to acceptable-use policies and should not be used for personal gaming or activities that could expose the device to non-corporate software and security risks. Personal activities should be done on personal devices.

prompt: An employee posts a photo on social media from the company's new product launch event. The photo clearly shows a whiteboard in the background with competitor analysis data and planned launch dates. What did the employee do wrong?
options: He posted without tagging his colleagues
He accidentally revealed confidential business strategy information to the public by posting a photo with sensitive data visible in the background
He posted before the official company announcement
He used a personal social media account instead of the company's account
explanation: Always check the full background of any photo taken in a work environment before posting publicly. Visible documents, screens, or whiteboards can accidentally disclose confidential information to competitors or the public.

prompt: You receive an automated email saying a large file has been shared with you via your company's file-sharing system. The link in the email takes you to a login page, but the URL contains 'sharepoint.company.com.files-hosted.net.' What should you do?
options: Log in â€” it looks like SharePoint
Log in but immediately change your password afterwards
Do not log in. The domain is not your company's official domain. Report the email to IT Security
Forward to IT and wait for a response before deciding
explanation: The URL uses your company's name as a prefix to an unrelated domain. This is a spoofed login page designed to steal your credentials. Report it to IT immediately â€” do not enter any information.

prompt: You realise you have been sending weekly project updates to the wrong email address for a month. The emails contained project timelines and internal cost estimates. What should you do?
options: Send the correct person all the emails and hope they understand
Stop sending to the wrong address, inform your manager, check whether a data breach needs to be reported, and ask IT to help investigate any existing sent items
Resend all emails to the correct address and continue
Ask the wrong recipient to delete the emails
explanation: Sending confidential data to the wrong recipient is a data breach. Depending on the sensitivity and volume of information, it may need to be reported to your data protection officer. Stop, inform your manager, and follow your company's breach response process.

prompt: Your colleague is on the phone discussing a sensitive employee grievance case. You notice she is speaking loudly and can be clearly heard by people at nearby desks. What should you do?
options: Listen carefully â€” this might be useful context for the team
Discreetly signal to her that she can be overheard, or suggest she move to a private room
Ask her to put the call on hold while you raise a concern
Send an email to HR noting what you heard
explanation: Grievance cases are highly confidential. A quiet, discreet signal is helpful and appropriate. Sensitive HR calls should be taken in a private meeting room or equivalent enclosed space.

prompt: A supplier emails your procurement team saying that due to a new regulation, all suppliers must provide a copy of their company's bank mandate form. The email includes a form to complete and return by email. What should your team do?
options: Complete and return the form since it is a regulatory requirement
Call the supplier on their verified number to confirm whether this request is genuine before completing any form
Email the supplier back asking for more information about the regulation
Forward the request to your manager who can decide
explanation: Forms requesting banking or financial details are frequently used in fraud. A phone call to the supplier using a number from your existing records â€” not from the email â€” will quickly confirm whether the request is genuine.

prompt: During a fire drill, employees leave the building quickly and most leave their computers unlocked with screens visible. A visitor who was waiting in reception moves freely through the empty open-plan office. What security lapse occurred?
options: The fire drill was not announced in advance
Unlocked workstations and an unescorted visitor in an empty office created both a data and physical security vulnerability
Employees did not take their laptops with them
The visitor should have evacuated too
explanation: Emergency evacuations must be considered in security planning. Unescorted visitors in empty offices with visible, unlocked screens present significant risks. Visitors should be escorted out by staff, and screens should auto-lock quickly.

prompt: You are asked to review and sign off on a third-party vendor's data security questionnaire. The vendor claims they encrypt all data at rest and in transit but cannot provide evidence or a certification. What should you do?
options: Accept their word â€” most vendors do this
Approve the questionnaire with a note that evidence is pending
Decline to approve the questionnaire until the vendor provides verifiable evidence such as a recent security audit report or recognised certification
Ask the vendor to email a summary instead of a certificate
explanation: Security claims without evidence are meaningless. Accepting unverified claims exposes your company if the vendor suffers a breach. Always require documented evidence before approving.

prompt: An employee applies for a role at another company and lists your company's client names and revenue figures in their application portfolio without asking permission. What did the employee do wrong?
options: They applied for a job without notifying their current manager
They disclosed confidential client information and commercial data to an external party without authorisation
They used work time to apply for jobs
They should have listed the clients by sector rather than by name
explanation: Client names and revenue data are confidential commercial information. Disclosing them in a personal job application shares proprietary company information with an external organisation and may violate confidentiality agreements.

prompt: You receive a message in your company's internal chat from a user called IT_Admin_Support asking you to click a link to validate your account before tomorrow's system upgrade. What should you do?
options: Click the link and complete the validation quickly
Reply to the message asking for more details
Do not click the link. Contact IT through official channels to verify whether a system upgrade is planned and whether any user action is genuinely required
Ignore the message and see if others receive it too
explanation: Internal chat accounts can be compromised or spoofed. Legitimate IT communications about system upgrades are usually sent through official channels, not direct messages with links. Verify through the IT helpdesk directly.

prompt: An accounts payable clerk receives an email from an unknown external address saying a supplier has changed their name and all future invoices will come from a new company entity with different bank details. The clerk updates the system immediately. What did she do wrong?
options: She should have asked for the request in writing
She updated supplier records and banking details based solely on an unsolicited email without independently verifying the change with the supplier
She should have involved her manager before making system changes
She should have archived the old supplier record before creating a new one
explanation: Supplier record changes â€” especially banking details â€” must be verified by calling the supplier on a known, pre-existing number. Acting on an unsolicited email alone is a serious financial control failure that could redirect payments to fraudsters.

prompt: You are about to leave a meeting room and notice the previous occupants have left a flipchart visible with a handwritten organisation chart showing names, titles, and reporting lines. What should you do?
options: Leave it â€” the cleaner will deal with it
Take a photo for reference
Tear off or erase the sheet so the information is not visible to the next group to use the room
Report it to HR
explanation: Organisational charts with names and reporting lines are sensitive HR and business information. Leaving them visible in shared spaces means visitors or unauthorised staff could see and misuse them. Remove or destroy them before leaving.

prompt: You receive an out-of-hours call from an unknown number. The caller says he is from your company's security operations centre and needs your Active Directory password to investigate a live breach. What should you do?
options: Provide the password â€” a live breach is serious
Provide only your username
Refuse. No legitimate security team member will ask for your password. Tell the caller you will call back through the official IT Security number, then do so to verify the situation
Give a temporary password and change it right after the call
explanation: Legitimate security teams do not need your password â€” they have other administrative tools. Urgency and authority are manipulation tactics. Always hang up and call back through a verified number you look up yourself.

prompt: You receive an email from 'facilities@yourcompany.com' saying the fire exit door sensor near your floor is being tested and will be unlocked all afternoon. The email asks you to keep the door propped open to assist engineers. What should you do?
options: Keep the door propped open as instructed
Verify the request with the facilities management team directly using their known internal number before propping open any security door
Email facilities back asking for more information
Ignore the email and let others decide
explanation: Even emails from apparently internal addresses can be spoofed. Propping open a security door without verification creates a physical access vulnerability. Confirm directly with facilities management using a number from your internal directory.

prompt: An employee in accounts payable receives an email from the company director's email address asking her to process an urgent payment to a new overseas supplier before close of business. The email says to keep the transaction confidential. What should she do?
options: Process it â€” the director's email confirms it is genuine
Process it but inform the finance manager afterwards
Do not process the payment. The combination of urgency, a new account, and a confidentiality instruction are major red flags. Verify face-to-face or by phone using a known number
Ask the director to resend from her personal email to double-check
explanation: Urgency plus secrecy plus a new payee is a classic fraud pattern. Email accounts can be compromised or spoofed. Always verify unusual or high-value payment requests through a separate, trusted channel, regardless of who the apparent sender is.

prompt: You log in to your email first thing in the morning and find a password reset email that you did not request. What should you do immediately?
options: Complete the reset since it is already in your inbox
Ignore it â€” it is probably a system glitch
Do not click the reset link. Change your password immediately through the official portal and report the unrequested reset to IT Security
Forward it to IT and wait for their instructions before doing anything
explanation: An unrequested password reset email means someone may have initiated the process using your account. Act fast â€” change your password through the official login page and alert IT Security so they can investigate whether your account has been targeted.

prompt: The administration team needs to store scanned copies of employee passport and ID documents collected during on-boarding. A team member saves them all to a shared departmental folder accessible to 40 people across the company. What did she do wrong?
options: She stored the documents digitally instead of keeping the originals
She saved highly sensitive personal identity documents to a broadly shared folder rather than a restricted, access-controlled location
She did not rename the files to a standard naming convention
She should have asked HR's permission before scanning
explanation: Passport and identity documents are among the most sensitive personal data a company holds. They must be stored in a restricted location with access limited to only those with a genuine need, in compliance with data protection regulations.

prompt: You receive an internal email from the company director's email asking you to approve a new supplier and add them to the payment system urgently. What should you do first?
options: Approve the supplier immediately to meet the deadline
Approve provisionally and email the director for confirmation
Pause the request and call or speak directly to the director to verify the instruction before making any system changes
Forward the request to the finance manager and let them action it
explanation: Urgent supplier addition requests, even from senior-seeming senders, should always be verified through a direct, trusted communication channel. Email alone is insufficient authorisation for adding new payees to financial systems.

prompt: Your company's expense system emails you to say your submitted expense claim has been rejected and you must re-upload your receipts by clicking a button in the email. The sending address is 'noreply@expense-claims-system.net.' What should you do?
options: Click the button and re-upload your receipts quickly
Do not click the button. Log in to the expense system directly using your bookmarked URL to check the status of your claim
Reply to the email asking why your claim was rejected
Call the finance team to report the rejection
explanation: The sending domain is not your company's official domain. Rather than clicking links in potentially spoofed emails, navigate directly to the expense system using a URL you know is correct. This avoids the risk of entering credentials on a fake page.

prompt: You are processing a new joiner's access permissions. Their manager has verbally told you to give them full access to the HR system. What should you do before granting access?
options: Grant full access since a manager requested it
Grant partial access and ask for more clarity later
Request a formal written access authorisation from the manager and confirm the access level is appropriate for the new joiner's role before granting it
Ask the new joiner what access they need and grant that
explanation: Access to systems â€” especially sensitive ones like HR â€” must be granted based on documented, role-appropriate authorisation. Verbal requests are insufficient. Access levels should follow the principle of minimum necessary access.

prompt: An employee sends a bulk email to all company staff reminding them about a team event. She accidentally includes an attachment containing the company's internal salary banding spreadsheet. What should she do as soon as she realises?
options: Send a follow-up email asking people not to open the attachment
Immediately notify her manager and IT, follow the company's data breach reporting process, and ask IT to recall the email if possible
Send another email to all staff explaining it was a mistake
Do nothing and hope nobody opens the attachment
explanation: Accidental disclosure of salary data to all staff is a data breach. It must be reported immediately through proper channels. IT should attempt to recall the email. Doing nothing or simply asking people not to look is insufficient.

prompt: You receive an email with the subject line 'Your leave balance will reset in 48 hours â€” act now' and a link to check your balance. The email appears to come from your HR system. What should you do?
options: Click the link immediately to check your balance before it resets
Open the HR portal directly via your bookmarked URL and check your leave balance there, without clicking the link in the email
Forward it to HR to confirm
Click the link on your mobile rather than your work laptop to be safer
explanation: Urgency-based emails with links are a common credential-harvesting technique. Regardless of how genuine the email looks, always navigate to internal systems using your known, bookmarked URL â€” not by clicking links in emails.

prompt: You are about to travel internationally for a business trip. Your manager suggests you take your personal laptop rather than your work laptop to avoid losing important company files. What should you tell your manager?
options: Agree â€” personal devices are less likely to be targeted
Agree but set up a work email on your personal laptop first
Explain that using personal devices for company work violates acceptable-use policy and puts company data outside of security controls; request a company-issued travel laptop instead
Use the personal laptop but only access company email, not files
explanation: Personal laptops lack corporate security controls such as encryption, remote wipe, and monitored access. Using them for business puts company data at serious risk. A company-issued device configured for travel is the correct solution.

prompt: A colleague tells you she has figured out how to access a shared network drive restricted to the finance team by using a shortcut another colleague sent her. She says it saves her time. What should you do?
options: Ask her to share the workaround with you
Ignore it â€” she is not doing anything harmful
Advise her to stop using the workaround immediately and report the access control gap to IT Security so it can be properly fixed
Tell her manager informally
explanation: Circumventing access controls â€” even accidentally through a shortcut â€” is a security issue regardless of intent. The gap must be reported so it can be closed. If the colleague genuinely needs the access, she should request it formally.

prompt: You are doing a video interview with a job candidate. Behind you, a whiteboard showing your team's project roadmap and key milestones is clearly visible on camera. What should you have done before the call?
options: Used a virtual background to blur it
Checked your background before the call and either removed the whiteboard content or moved to a neutral background
Asked the candidate to sign an NDA before the interview
Positioned your camera higher to hide the whiteboard
explanation: Before any video call with external parties, check what is visible in your background. Confidential information on whiteboards, screens, or desks may be clearly visible on camera to people outside the company.

prompt: You notice that the same employee badge has been used to badge in at the front entrance and badge out at the back car park simultaneously, which is physically impossible. What should you do?
options: Assume it is a system error and do nothing
Report the anomaly to IT Security or the building security team immediately as it may indicate badge cloning or a system compromise
Mention it to the badge holder to see if they have an explanation
Log it in your notebook in case it comes up again
explanation: Simultaneous access events at different locations using the same badge indicate either badge cloning â€” a serious physical security threat â€” or a system fault. Either way, it must be reported to security immediately for investigation.

prompt: A purchasing manager receives an email from a known supplier with a new contact person's name and a request to communicate all future orders through a new personal Gmail address. What should the purchasing manager do?
options: Update the contact details and use the new Gmail address going forward
Reply to the email confirming the change
Call the supplier on the existing verified number to confirm whether the contact change is genuine before updating any records or sending future communications
Ask the new contact to send an introductory email from the new Gmail account first
explanation: A supplier suddenly requesting communications through a personal Gmail rather than a company email is a significant red flag. Verify the change by calling the supplier directly through your existing contact number before acting on any such request.

prompt: Your company has a policy that employees must not install unapproved software on work devices. A colleague installs a free productivity app she found online without submitting an IT approval request. What did she do wrong?
options: She should have paid for the app instead of using a free version
She installed software that has not been vetted for security, potentially introducing vulnerabilities or prohibited functionality to a company device
She did not tell her manager before installing
Free software is fine â€” she only violated policy on a technicality
explanation: Unapproved software can contain security flaws, collect data without consent, or conflict with corporate systems. The IT approval process exists to vet applications before they are installed on devices that handle company data.

prompt: You receive an email from the HR system saying your employment contract has been updated and is ready to review. You are asked to log in via a link in the email. You were not told by HR that any changes were being made. What should you do?
options: Log in to review the contract since HR may have updated it without notifying you
Do not click the link. Contact HR directly through internal channels to ask whether your contract has genuinely been updated and get the correct access method
Click the link but read the contract without accepting or signing anything
Forward the email to your manager and ask if they are aware of any changes
explanation: Unexpected emails about contract changes should be verified with HR directly before you act on any links. Credential phishing often mimics HR systems because employees instinctively open such messages. Confirm the update through a trusted internal contact first.

prompt: The accounts payable team receives an invoice for a significant amount from a supplier for services described only as 'Consultancy â€” October.' There is no purchase order reference on the invoice. What should the team do?
options: Pay it â€” the amount is within normal range
Contact the supplier to ask them to add a PO number, then pay
Do not pay the invoice without a valid purchase order reference. Verify with the relevant department whether the services were authorised before processing payment
Approve it if no one objects within three business days
explanation: Invoices without purchase order references bypass the company's procurement authorisation process. This is a financial control safeguard â€” paying without a matching PO makes it impossible to verify that goods or services were legitimately ordered.

prompt: An employee in administration is asked to book a venue for the company's annual conference. She finds a great price through a website she does not usually use and pays using the company credit card without getting a quote from at least one other supplier. What policy has she likely violated?
options: She booked without using an approved travel agent
She likely bypassed the company's procurement policy requiring competitive quotes or a minimum number of supplier bids for purchases above a certain threshold
She should have used the company's preferred venue
She did not inform the events committee before booking
explanation: Most companies require competitive quotes for purchases above a defined value. Booking directly without comparison bids bypasses procurement controls designed to ensure value for money and prevent conflicts of interest.

prompt: You receive a voicemail from someone claiming to be from HMRC saying your company owes unpaid taxes and you must call a number immediately or face legal action. The tone is threatening. What should you do?
options: Call the number immediately to clarify the situation
Pass the voicemail to your finance director to call back
Do not call the number. Contact HMRC directly using the official number from the GOV.UK website to verify whether any such demand exists
Ignore it â€” HMRC always writes formally
explanation: Threatening voicemails impersonating tax authorities are a common fraud tactic. Always verify through the official government website contact details, never by calling numbers provided in unsolicited voicemails.

prompt: You are told by IT that you must reset your work password within 24 hours due to a routine security policy update. You choose 'Summer2024!' as your new password. What is wrong with this choice?
options: It is too short
It contains a predictable word and number pattern that is easy to guess and appears on common password lists
It should not contain special characters
Seasonal passwords expire too quickly
explanation: Passwords based on seasons, years, or common words followed by numbers are among the first combinations tried in automated attacks. A strong password should be long, random, and not based on predictable patterns. Use a passphrase or a password manager.

prompt: A colleague is leaving for maternity leave and asks you to keep using her login credentials to access the system she manages so nothing gets disrupted while she is away. What should you do?
options: Agree â€” it is just temporary
Use her credentials but only for read access
Decline. Using another employee's credentials is a policy violation regardless of the reason. Ask IT to assign you your own appropriate access if you need it
Agree but change her password so only you know it
explanation: Sharing login credentials â€” even temporarily between colleagues â€” is a policy violation that destroys individual accountability. Any actions taken using shared credentials cannot be attributed correctly. Ensure IT grants you your own proper access.

prompt: You receive an email with an invoice attached from a company claiming to be a new cleaning contractor who was approved last week by your facilities manager. You have no record of this approval. What do you do?
options: Pay it since the facilities manager handles cleaners
Call the facilities manager on a known number to verify whether the contractor was genuinely approved before processing any payment
Email the sender to ask for a contract copy and then pay
Hold the payment for two weeks and see if a follow-up comes
explanation: Invoices from vendors you cannot verify must not be paid without confirmation. Always verify new vendor approvals through an internal contact â€” not through any contact details provided by the vendor â€” before releasing payment.

prompt: You finish a sensitive client meeting in a conference room and close your laptop. The previous presenter's slides, which contain client revenue data, are still being displayed on the room's shared screen. What should you do?
options: Leave it â€” the meeting is over
Disconnect the display or turn off the screen so the data is no longer visible before leaving the room
Take a photo for reference and then leave
Email the previous presenter to remotely disconnect their slides
explanation: Shared display screens in meeting rooms remain visible to anyone entering after the meeting ends. Always disconnect the display or turn off the screen before leaving to prevent confidential data from being seen by subsequent users.

prompt: Your department head sends you a message via personal WhatsApp â€” not the approved company messaging tool â€” asking you to approve a purchase order and send her the signed PDF. What should you do?
options: Approve and send it since she is your department head
Send a lower-value version first and ask for her to confirm on the official channel before sending the full document
Decline to share company documents via personal messaging apps and ask her to use the approved company channel instead
Approve the order internally but only tell her verbally
explanation: Company documents â€” especially signed financial approvals â€” must be handled only through approved, secure business channels. Personal messaging apps lack the security and audit controls required for business-critical transactions.

prompt: An HR officer is asked to provide a reference for a former employee. The requesting employer asks for the former employee's exact salary during employment. What should the HR officer do?
options: Provide the salary since it helps the former employee get a fair offer
Provide a salary range rather than the exact figure
Only provide information the former employee has explicitly consented to share, and check the company's reference policy before disclosing any salary information
Decline to provide any reference at all
explanation: Salary information is sensitive personal data. Disclosing it to a third party requires the individual's consent. HR officers must follow the company's reference policy and applicable data protection law before sharing any personal details about former employees.

prompt: The CFO sends an email marked URGENT asking you to wire Â£42,000 to a new overseas account before 3 p.m. because a deal is closing today. She says to skip the usual approval process this once. What should you do?
options: Wire the funds immediately â€” the CFO has authority to approve payments
Wire half now and hold the rest until you hear back
Do not process the payment. Call the CFO directly on her known office number to confirm the instruction before taking any action
Email the CFO back asking for written authorisation, then wire once she replies
explanation: Urgent payment requests that bypass normal controls are a classic fraud pattern. A CFO's email address can be spoofed or compromised. Always verify extraordinary payment requests by calling the person directly on a number you already have on record.

prompt: A vendor your company has paid for two years emails to say they have switched banks and asks you to update their account details before this month's payment run. The email looks identical to their usual correspondence. What is your next step?
options: Update the details right away to avoid a late payment
Update the details but flag it in the payment notes
Do not update anything yet. Call the vendor using the phone number you have in your existing records to confirm the change is genuine
Reply to the email asking the vendor to confirm the new details in writing
explanation: Fraudsters intercept or impersonate supplier email to reroute payments. The only safe way to verify a bank detail change is to call the vendor using a contact number you already have â€” never use any number or email provided in the suspect message.

prompt: An invoice arrives by email from a supplier you recognise, but this time it has a PDF attachment called 'FINAL_INVOICE_OPEN_IMMEDIATELY.pdf' that you were not expecting. What should you do before opening it?
options: Open it â€” the supplier is known and invoices are expected
Open it on your personal phone to keep the work system safe
Do not open the attachment. Contact the supplier through a known phone number or email to confirm they sent it, then open it only after verification
Forward it to your manager and ask them to open it first
explanation: Unexpected attachments with urgent-sounding filenames are a common delivery method for harmful software, even when they appear to come from known senders. Verify with the supplier directly before opening any attachment you were not expecting.

prompt: You receive a phone call from someone who introduces himself as your company's external auditor. He says he needs your accounts payable login credentials to access the payment system for an unannounced audit. What should you do?
options: Provide the credentials since auditors need system access
Give him view-only access credentials only
Refuse. Legitimate auditors use formal channels and do not ask for staff login credentials. Tell him you will pass the request to your finance director and hang up
Ask him to email you from an official address before providing anything
explanation: Auditors access systems through formally arranged processes and never require individual employee login credentials. Any caller requesting your password or system access should be treated with suspicion. Escalate through your finance leadership immediately.

prompt: Your line manager sends you a WhatsApp message asking you to purchase five Â£100 Amazon gift cards for a client thank-you gift and send him the redemption codes right away. You have never done this before. What should you do?
options: Buy the gift cards â€” your manager has asked and it is for a client
Buy two gift cards and ask for more information before buying the rest
Do not buy anything. Call your manager directly on his office or mobile number to verify the request before spending any company money
Ask your manager to send the request through the official expense system first
explanation: Gift card requests sent via personal messaging apps are a well-known fraud technique. A fraudster impersonates a manager to get untraceable funds quickly. Always call the apparent sender using a verified number before acting on any financial request made outside official channels.

prompt: A new invoice for Â£6,800 arrives from a company called 'Apex Consulting Services' for strategic advisory work in October. No one in your team has heard of this company and there is no purchase order on file. What should you do?
options: Pay it â€” the description sounds plausible and the amount is under the approval limit
Hold the payment and ask your manager to approve it verbally
Do not pay the invoice. Raise a query internally to find out whether anyone authorised this work, and require a valid purchase order before processing payment
Ask the vendor to resubmit with more detail, then pay
