explanation: Paying an invoice for a company or service with no corresponding purchase order or internal approval is a serious financial control failure. All payments should be matched to an authorised purchase order and a verified business relationship.

prompt: You receive a call from someone who says she is the new accounts manager at one of your major suppliers. She says the supplier's payment terms have changed and future invoices must be paid within seven days or a penalty applies. She gives you a new email address to send remittance advice to. What should you do?
options: Update the payment terms and new email in the system â€” she is a supplier contact
Update the email address only and keep the existing terms
Do not make any changes based on this call. Tell her you will verify the changes with your existing supplier contact through your usual communication channel before updating anything
Ask her to send a written request to your existing supplier email and then update the records
explanation: Unsolicited calls asking you to change supplier contact details or payment terms are often used to redirect payment notifications and funds. Verify all changes using existing, independently verified supplier contact details.

prompt: While processing end-of-month payments, you notice a payment run last month included a transfer of Â£9,500 to a vendor whose name is slightly different from the approved supplier list â€” 'Grafix Solutions Ltd' instead of 'Graphics Solutions Ltd.' What should you do?
options: Assume it is the same company with a name change and move on
Note the discrepancy and raise it at the next team meeting
Immediately flag the payment to your finance manager and compliance team for investigation â€” a mismatched vendor name is a sign of a potentially fraudulent transaction
Ask the vendor to confirm their registered name by email
explanation: A small variation in a vendor's registered name can indicate a fraudulent entity has been inserted into the payment system. This must be investigated promptly â€” not noted for a future meeting â€” as funds may have already been misdirected.

prompt: The head of operations calls you urgently, saying a supplier has threatened to stop services unless an overdue invoice of Â£18,000 is paid today. He asks you to process it without going through the normal three-way matching process. What should you do?
options: Process it â€” a service disruption would be worse than skipping a process step
Pay half now and the rest after the matching is done

Decline to bypass the approval process. Explain that every payment must follow controls regardless of urgency, and offer to escalate to the finance director to resolve it quickly through proper channels
Pay it but document that the matching process was skipped
explanation: Financial controls such as three-way matching exist specifically to prevent fraud and errors. Urgency is one of the most common reasons cited to bypass controls â€” and one of the most common fraud tactics. Escalate rather than override.

prompt: An email arrives in the finance inbox appearing to be from the CEO, asking accounts payable to set up a new vendor â€” a law firm â€” and process a payment of Â£25,000 marked as legally sensitive. The CEO asks for strict confidentiality. What should you do?
options: Set up the vendor and process the payment â€” the CEO's instruction must be followed
Set up the vendor but hold the payment until you can confirm
Do not act on this email. Confidentiality instructions combined with urgency and a new vendor are major red flags. Verify in person or by phone with the CEO or the legal team before taking any action
Email the CEO back asking for a formal purchase order
explanation: Requests combining urgency, a new payee, confidentiality instructions, and a high value are consistent with executive impersonation fraud. No legitimate instruction bypasses financial controls entirely. Verify directly and in person when possible.

prompt: You are processing a batch of invoices and notice one from a supplier is for exactly Â£4,999 â€” just under the Â£5,000 limit that requires a second approver. This is the third invoice from this supplier in the past month, each just under the limit. What should you do?
options: Process all three since each invoice is individually within the approval limit
Process two and query the third
Pause all three payments and escalate to your finance manager. Multiple invoices structured just below an approval threshold is a known warning sign of invoice fraud
Ask the supplier to combine the invoices into one and resubmit
explanation: Submitting multiple invoices just below an approval threshold â€” known as invoice splitting â€” is a technique used to avoid financial controls. Identifying this pattern and escalating it promptly is an important fraud-prevention responsibility.

prompt: A caller says he is from your bank's fraud prevention team and that your company's business account has been targeted. He asks you to transfer all funds to a 'safe holding account' he will give you the details for. What should you do?
options: Transfer the funds immediately â€” protecting the account is the priority
Transfer only a portion to test the account first
Hang up immediately. Banks never ask you to move funds to a new account. Call your bank back using the official number on their website or your bank card to verify
Ask the caller to send confirmation of the request by email before transferring
explanation: This is a classic authorised push payment fraud script. No legitimate bank will ever ask you to move money to a new account for security reasons. Always call back using the official number from your bank card or the bank's official website â€” never a number the caller gives you.

prompt: An email arrives from 'payments@your-company.co.uk' â€” note the hyphen â€” asking all staff to confirm their bank details for an upcoming salary adjustment. The email looks professional and is addressed to you personally. What should you do?
options: Submit your bank details â€” the email is addressed to you personally and looks official
Submit only your account number, not your sort code
Do not submit anything. The domain has a hyphen that is not in your company's real domain. Report the email to IT Security immediately
Reply asking the sender to confirm which department sent it
explanation: A hyphenated domain is not your company's domain. This is a look-alike domain designed to fool quick readers. Legitimate payroll teams never collect bank details via email. Report it to IT and verify with HR directly using known internal contact details.

prompt: You receive an invoice via email with a PDF attachment. When you open the PDF, a pop-up appears asking you to enable editing to view the full invoice. What should you do?
options: Click Enable Editing â€” you need to see the full invoice
Click Enable Editing but close the document immediately after
Close the document without enabling anything and report the invoice email to IT Security
Print the PDF without enabling editing so the content cannot run
explanation: Pop-ups in PDFs asking you to enable editing or content are a mechanism for running harmful code on your device. A legitimate invoice never requires you to enable any feature to view it. Close the document and report the email immediately.

prompt: You are finalising a large payment to a contractor and the contractor calls to give you a different bank account number than the one on the invoice, saying it is more convenient for them. What should you do?
options: Use the new number â€” the contractor called personally to give it
Use the number on the invoice since that was already verified
Do not change the banking details based on a phone call alone. Ask the contractor to submit a formal written request through your standard vendor-change process before updating any records
Pay half to each account to be safe
explanation: Verbal bank detail changes â€” even from a call that seems to come from the contractor â€” are easily faked. Any change to payment details must go through a documented, verifiable process. Pay to the invoice details while the change is formally processed.

prompt: The managing director sends you a text message asking you to make an urgent payment of Â£8,000 to a personal account belonging to a client while he is out of the country. He says he cannot get to email. What should you do?
options: Process the payment â€” the MD's number is in your phone contacts
Process it and confirm back to the MD by text once done

Do not process the payment. Text messages are not a secure or verifiable payment instruction. Call the MD on his known number and verify through the official finance approval process before taking action
Ask the MD to email the request when he gets access to email
explanation: Payment instructions sent via personal text message are not a secure channel and cannot be sufficiently verified. Urgency plus an unusual personal account destination plus an inability to use normal channels are all red flags. Verify directly before any payment.

prompt: A long-standing supplier sends a corrected invoice to replace one you already paid last week. The new invoice has the same reference number and amount but different bank details. What should you do?
options: Pay the corrected invoice to the new account since the supplier says it is an update
Ignore the new invoice since the original was already paid
Do not pay until you have called the supplier on their known number to confirm whether the original payment was received and whether the new bank details are genuinely theirs
Email the supplier asking which account to use and pay once they respond
explanation: Resubmitting an already-paid invoice with new bank details is a common fraud method. Always call the supplier using your existing contact details to confirm whether the first payment arrived and whether the new account details are legitimate.

prompt: A member of your accounts team processes a payment to a vendor and later realises the vendor's bank account number was changed in the system two days ago by an unknown user. What should happen first?
options: Contact the vendor to ask if the change was made by them
Process the next payment as normal and investigate the change later
Immediately escalate to the finance manager and IT Security, freeze further payments to that vendor, and investigate who made the change and when
Revert the account number to the original and continue
explanation: An unauthorised change to vendor bank details is a serious security incident that may mean funds have been misdirected. It must be escalated immediately to both finance leadership and IT Security, and further payments frozen until the investigation is complete.

prompt: You receive an email from a supplier you regularly pay, but this time the email address is 'invoices@suppliernane.com' instead of 'invoices@suppliername.com' â€” one letter is different. The invoice amount and format look normal. What should you do?
options: Pay it â€” the amount and format are correct
Pay it but make a note of the address difference
Do not pay. Contact the supplier using your existing contact details to confirm whether this invoice is genuine before making any payment
Reply to the email asking the supplier to confirm the address change
explanation: A one-letter difference in an email domain is a tell-tale sign of a look-alike address used to intercept payments. Never pay based on a suspicious sending address alone. Contact the real supplier directly using contact details from your records.

prompt: At the end of the financial year, your finance director asks you to post an accounting entry to move Â£30,000 of expenses into the next financial period so that this year's figures look better. What should you do?
options: Post the entry â€” the finance director is your senior and has approved it
Post the entry but flag it in your personal notes
Decline to post an entry that misrepresents the timing of expenses. Explain that this would be inaccurate reporting and raise the concern with your compliance officer or external auditor if pressured
Post the entry only if it is under the materiality threshold
explanation: Deliberately deferring expenses to improve financial results is earnings manipulation and may constitute fraud. Employees are never obligated to follow instructions that require them to falsify financial records, regardless of seniority. Report the request through your compliance or ethics channel.

prompt: You receive a call from someone who identifies himself as a partner at your company's law firm. He says a highly confidential legal settlement requires an immediate transfer and asks for your company's bank account number and payment authorisation code. What should you do?
options: Provide the details since legal matters can be sensitive and time-critical
Provide the account number but not the authorisation code
Refuse. Tell the caller you will call the law firm's main office using the number on their official website to verify the request before providing any information
Ask the caller to email you from his law firm email address before proceeding
explanation: Impersonating legal or professional advisors is a known fraud tactic used to extract financial information under the cover of confidentiality. Always call back through the firm's publicly listed main number to verify any such request before sharing any financial details.

prompt: Your company's accounts payable team receives the same invoice from a supplier twice â€” once by post and once by email, but the email version has different bank details from the posted version. What should the team do?
options: Pay the posted version since physical invoices are more trustworthy
Pay the email version since it arrived more recently
Do not pay either version yet. Call the supplier using your existing contact details to confirm which version is correct and which bank account to use
Pay both and request a credit note for the duplicate
explanation: Receiving two versions of the same invoice with different bank details is a strong signal of attempted payment fraud. Neither version should be paid until the correct details are confirmed directly with the supplier through an independently verified contact.

prompt: A new member of the finance team is given access to the payment system and, in her first week, processes a large payment on her own without a second approver because she did not know it was required. What went wrong in this situation?
options: The new employee should have asked a colleague to double-check the amount
The company failed to properly communicate and enforce dual-authorisation controls before giving the employee payment access
The employee should have flagged the payment as a query rather than processing it
The finance manager should have reviewed all first-week transactions
explanation: Access to payment systems should only be granted after full training on approval controls. Giving a new employee payment-processing access before they understand the required authorisation steps â€” such as dual approval for high-value transactions â€” is a process failure by the company.

prompt: You are about to pay a supplier's invoice and notice their registered address on the invoice is different from the address you have on file. The invoice arrived by email. What should you do before paying?
options: Pay it â€” companies sometimes change address without notifying all contacts
Update the address in the system and pay
Hold the payment and call the supplier using your existing contact number to confirm whether they have moved and whether the invoice is genuine
Email the supplier asking them to confirm their current address before you pay
explanation: A different address on an invoice from what you have on file is a discrepancy worth investigating before payment. Call the supplier using the number you already have on record â€” not any number on the invoice itself â€” to confirm.

prompt: A senior manager asks you to process a personal expense claim he submitted on behalf of a colleague, signing both names on the form. What is wrong with this situation?
options: Expense claims must always be printed, not handwritten
The colleague's claim should be submitted under the colleague's own name and signature â€” signing on someone else's behalf misrepresents who incurred the expense and who is authorising it
Expenses can only be processed at the end of the month
A senior manager is not authorised to submit expense claims on behalf of colleagues
explanation: Each expense claim must be submitted and signed by the person who incurred the cost. Signing on behalf of another person creates a false record, removes accountability, and may be used to conceal misuse of company funds.

prompt: You receive an email from what appears to be your company's bank, asking you to re-authorise a pending payment by clicking a link and entering your payment portal credentials. The payment is described as urgent. What should you do?
options: Click the link and re-authorise to avoid the payment failing
Click the link but use a different password to test if it is genuine
Do not click the link. Log in to your payment portal directly using your bookmarked URL and check whether any payment actually requires re-authorisation
Forward the email to the bank's support team and wait for confirmation
explanation: Banks do not re-authorise payments via links sent by email. This is a credential phishing attempt. Always go directly to your payment portal using a URL you know is genuine â€” never via links in unexpected emails.

prompt: An employee in accounts payable is the only person who processes payments on Fridays when her manager is out. She receives a call from the CEO asking her to transfer Â£50,000 immediately and not to mention it to her manager. What should she do?
options: Process the payment â€” refusing a CEO instruction could be a disciplinary matter
Process half and inform her manager on Monday
Refuse to process the payment without proper authorisation and tell the caller she must follow the company's dual-approval policy, regardless of who is asking
Process it and document that the CEO instructed her to do so
explanation: No one â€” including a CEO â€” has the authority to override financial controls, and any instruction to do so should raise immediate suspicion. An employee following procedure will never be disciplined for refusing to bypass a financial control. The instruction to keep it from her manager is a serious red flag.

prompt: You discover that a colleague in the finance team has been approving his own expense claims because the system allows it and his manager has been too busy to review them. What should be done immediately?
options: Ask the colleague to stop and have his manager review future claims
Report it to the finance director and request that system controls be updated to prevent self-approval of expenses
Ignore it if the expenses look reasonable
Ask the colleague to have a team member informally review claims instead
explanation: Self-approval of expense claims removes a critical financial control and creates an opportunity for misuse. The issue must be escalated so that system access controls are fixed and all previously self-approved claims are reviewed retrospectively.

prompt: A supplier calls to say they have not received payment for an invoice you processed last month. When you check the system, you see the payment went to a different account than the one on the invoice. What happened and what should you do now?
options: Tell the supplier to resubmit the invoice with correct details
Inform the supplier, immediately escalate to your finance manager, and investigate how the bank details in the system were changed and by whom
Process a second payment to the correct account and write off the first as a loss
Ask IT to look into the system discrepancy when they are next available
explanation: A payment made to an account different from the one on the invoice indicates the bank details were altered â€” potentially by a fraudster. This is a financial incident requiring immediate escalation, investigation of the account change, and likely involvement of your bank and police.

prompt: You process an invoice payment and receive a call from an unknown person who says he is with your bank's fraud team. He tells you the payment is on hold and you need to confirm your company's bank security code to release it. What should you do?
options: Give the code â€” the payment needs to go through
Give the last four digits of the code only
Hang up. Your bank will never ask for a security code by phone. Call your bank directly using the number on your card or their website to check if there is a genuine issue with the payment
Ask the caller to hold while you look up the code
explanation: This is a vishing script designed to extract security codes so a fraudster can authorise transactions or access accounts. Hang up and call your bank using their official number. Never provide security codes, PINs, or passwords to inbound callers.

prompt: A junior member of the finance team mentions he has been entering invoices received from a supplier he has a personal relationship with outside of work. He processes and approves these invoices himself. What is the issue?
options: He should not be processing invoices from companies he knows personally without declaring the relationship and having someone else approve
He is processing too many invoices manually instead of using automation
Knowing a supplier personally is helpful for the company â€” no issue here
He should disclose the relationship only if the invoice value is over a set threshold
explanation: Processing and approving invoices from a supplier with whom you have a personal relationship is a conflict of interest. It must be declared, and the approval should be handled by someone with no personal connection to that supplier.

prompt: You receive a call from a person claiming to be from HMRC saying your company has an outstanding VAT liability and must pay immediately via a bank transfer to an account she reads out. She says failing to pay today will result in penalties. What should you do?
options: Transfer the amount to avoid penalties
Ask for more time and transfer tomorrow
Do not make any transfer. Hang up and check your company's actual VAT position by logging into your HMRC online account. Contact HMRC using their official published number if needed
Ask the caller to send a letter with the payment details
explanation: HMRC does not collect tax payments through cold calls dictating bank transfer details. This is a common impersonation fraud. Always verify tax obligations through your HMRC online account and use only the contact details published on the official GOV.UK website.

prompt: The finance director asks you to make a payment to a vendor before the purchase order has been raised, saying the PO will follow next week. What should you do?
options: Process the payment since the finance director approved it verbally
Process it and make a note to match the PO when it arrives
Explain that payment before a purchase order is raised is against financial policy and request that the PO be raised first, or escalate to the CFO if the finance director insists
Process it as an emergency payment and document the reason
explanation: Purchase orders exist as a financial control to ensure every payment is pre-authorised. Paying before a PO is raised removes this control. No individual, regardless of seniority, should be able to consistently bypass procurement controls.

prompt: You are reviewing expense claims and notice that one employee has submitted restaurant receipts totalling Â£480 across three separate claims in one month, each just below the Â£200 limit requiring manager approval. What should you do?
options: Process all three since each is individually within the limit
Process two and query the third
Flag all three claims to the employee's manager for review â€” submitting multiple claims structured just below an approval limit is a warning sign of deliberate threshold avoidance
Ask the employee to justify the expenses in writing before processing
explanation: Splitting claims to keep each one below an approval threshold is a known method of avoiding financial oversight. When a pattern of just-below-limit submissions appears, it must be escalated to the relevant manager for review.

prompt: A supplier sends an email saying their accounting software has changed and all future remittance advice must be sent to a new email address at a different domain. What should you do before updating your records?
options: Update the email address right away to ensure they receive remittances
Update it and send a test remittance to confirm delivery
Call the supplier on your existing contact number to verify that the new email address is genuine before making any changes to their record
Reply to the email asking the supplier to confirm the address in writing
explanation: Changing remittance email addresses can be used by fraudsters to intercept payment confirmations and manipulate future transactions. Verify any contact detail changes by calling the supplier directly using your existing, verified contact number.

prompt: You receive a phone call from someone claiming to be a debt collection agency, saying your company owes money to a supplier and if you do not pay immediately the matter will be referred to court. The caller gives you an account number to pay into. What should you do?
options: Pay the amount to avoid legal action
Ask the caller to hold while you raise a payment

Do not pay. Tell the caller you will look into the matter through your own records. Research the debt collection agency's details independently and verify any genuine debt with your accounts team before making any payment
Ask the caller to send a letter and pay once it arrives
explanation: Fraudsters use fake debt collection threats to pressure companies into making immediate payments to fraudulent accounts. Verify any claimed debt against your own records and independently verify the agency before transferring any money.

prompt: You are the only person in the office and receive an urgent instruction by email â€” appearing to be from a board member â€” to release a payment before the end of business. You cannot reach anyone else for confirmation. What should you do?
options: Release the payment â€” the board member's email is authority enough
Release it and send an apology note if it turns out to be wrong

Do not release the payment without confirmation. Wait until you can reach another authorised person, even if the deadline passes. The financial risk of a fraudulent payment outweighs a delayed legitimate one
Release half the payment and hold the rest
explanation: Being isolated and under time pressure are deliberate elements of payment fraud. A missed deadline is recoverable; a misdirected payment often is not. No payment that cannot be properly authorised should be released, regardless of the apparent urgency.

prompt: An invoice arrives for software licences that your company has been paying for two years. This month the invoice total is 40% higher than usual with no explanation. What should you do before paying?
options: Pay it â€” licence costs go up over time
Pay it and query the increase with the supplier afterwards
Hold the payment and contact the supplier using your existing contact details to request a detailed breakdown of the increase before authorising payment
Pay the usual amount and dispute the difference in writing
explanation: A significant unexplained price increase on a recurring invoice is a red flag. It could indicate a fraudulent invoice or a supplier billing error. Always request a written breakdown and compare it against your contract terms before releasing payment.

prompt: A manager submits an expense claim for a business dinner that includes alcohol costs well above the company's policy limit. She says the client insisted on an expensive restaurant and it would have been rude to refuse. What should you do?
options: Reimburse the full amount since client entertainment has different rules
Reimburse up to the policy limit and ask the manager to absorb the rest

Decline to approve expenses beyond the policy limit regardless of the reason given, and advise the manager to seek a policy exception through the proper approval channel if she believes it is warranted
Split the claim into two separate submissions to bring each under the limit
explanation: Expense policies exist to control spending and ensure fairness. Approving over-limit expenses without formal exception approval undermines those controls. If an exception is warranted, it must be requested through the proper channel â€” not informally justified after the fact.

prompt: You notice that one of your company's recurring monthly payments â€” set up as an automated standing order â€” is going to a company you have no contract or invoice on file for. It has been running for eight months. What should you do?
options: Leave it running and investigate at the end of the financial year
Cancel the standing order immediately without informing anyone
Immediately flag this to your finance manager. A standing order with no supporting contract or invoices could indicate fraud, an error, or an unauthorised payment arrangement
Email the receiving company to ask what the payments are for
explanation: Standing orders without contracts or invoices represent an uncontrolled financial outflow. This should be escalated immediately â€” it could be a legitimate arrangement not properly documented, an old payment that was never cancelled, or active fraud.

prompt: You receive an email from a trusted colleague in a different office asking you to urgently process a refund payment to a customer using account details she has pasted into the email. She says the customer is very upset. What should you do?
options: Process the refund â€” the request is from a colleague and it is a customer refund
Process it but CC the customer on the payment confirmation
Verify the request by calling your colleague directly on her known number before processing any payment, to ensure the email genuinely came from her
Email your colleague back asking for confirmation and process the refund once she replies
explanation: Colleague email accounts can be compromised. Any request to send money â€” even a refund â€” should be verified by phone before processing. An email reply from a compromised account would simply come from the attacker.

prompt: A staff member in accounts submits expenses for a hotel stay during a conference. When you check, you find she also claimed the same hotel stay on a company credit card, meaning the stay has been claimed twice. What should you do?
options: Reimburse the expense claim and assume the credit card charge will be reconciled later
Reject one claim and process the other without raising it further
Reject the duplicate claim, inform the employee that a double claim has been identified, and flag it to the finance manager to determine whether it was accidental or deliberate
Ask the employee to provide additional receipts to clarify
explanation: Duplicate claims â€” whether accidental or deliberate â€” must be identified and escalated. The employee must be notified, the duplicate rejected, and the finance manager informed so any pattern of behaviour can be identified.

prompt: Your company receives a call from someone claiming to be a journalist investigating financial fraud at your organisation. He asks for details of recent large payments made. What should you do?
options: Share publicly available financial information to be cooperative
Refuse to share anything and hang up
Do not share any financial information. Direct the caller to your company's communications or legal team and report the call internally
Ask him to submit a formal information request in writing
explanation: Finance team members should never share payment or financial data with external parties, including media representatives. All external enquiries must be directed to your communications or legal team, and the call should be reported internally.

prompt: You are reviewing the company's monthly bank statement and find a small debit of Â£12 to an unknown company that has been recurring for six months. It is small enough that no one has noticed it. What should you do?
options: Ignore it â€” the amount is too small to be worth investigating
Note it and review again in six months
Investigate the charge immediately. Small, recurring debits to unknown payees can indicate an unauthorised direct debit or the early stages of a larger fraudulent scheme
Ask your bank to refund the last charge only
explanation: Small recurring charges from unrecognised companies should always be investigated promptly. They can be the result of an unauthorised direct debit, a subscription set up without authorisation, or an early indicator of larger financial fraud.

prompt: During an end-of-year audit, the auditor finds that several purchase orders were raised and approved by the same person. Company policy requires two different people to raise and approve a purchase order. What control failure does this represent?
options: The purchase orders were raised too close to the year end
The same person raising and approving their own purchase orders removes the independent check designed to prevent unauthorised or fraudulent spending
Purchase orders must always be digital, not handwritten
The auditor should have been notified about these purchase orders in advance
explanation: Segregation of duties requires that the person who initiates a financial transaction is different from the person who approves it. When the same person does both, there is no independent check â€” creating an opportunity for fraud or error to go undetected.

prompt: You receive an email from your company's CEO asking for a list of all employees who are currently on a personal improvement plan, along with their salaries. The email is sent from the CEO's company address. What should you do?
options: Send the list immediately â€” it is the CEO's company address
Send the list but remove salary information
Verify the request by calling the CEO directly. Even from an authentic-looking address, requests for sensitive HR data should be confirmed before sharing
Forward the request to HR and ask them to send the data directly
explanation: Even genuine-looking executive email accounts can be compromised. Sensitive HR and personal data should never be shared based on a single email request alone â€” particularly a request that combines multiple types of sensitive information. Verify directly.

prompt: A supplier contacts you to say they have not been paid for three invoices totalling Â£22,000. When you check, all three payments show as processed in your system. What should you do first?
options: Ask the supplier to re-raise the invoices
Resend all three payments immediately to avoid a dispute
Compare the bank account details the payments were sent to against the supplier's actual account number on file, and investigate whether the details in the system were altered
Ask the supplier to provide their bank statement to prove non-receipt
explanation: If payments were processed but not received by the supplier, it may mean the bank details in the system were changed by a fraudster. Before reprocessing, you must establish where the money actually went by checking whether the destination account details match the supplier's genuine details.

prompt: Your procurement system sends you an automated alert saying a new vendor has been added and a payment of Â£15,000 has already been authorised. You did not add this vendor or authorise this payment. What should you do?
options: Check with your team to see if someone else added the vendor
Cancel the vendor and note the alert in your records
Immediately escalate to IT Security and your finance manager, freeze the payment if possible, and treat this as a potential system breach or internal fraud
Email the vendor to ask them to explain how they were added
explanation: An unknown vendor added to the payment system with a large payment already authorised is a serious incident. It requires immediate escalation â€” payments could be directed to a fraudulent account. Time is critical if the payment has not yet been processed.

prompt: A salesperson in your company regularly submits mileage claims but does not keep a mileage log. She estimates the distances from memory. What is the problem with this?
options: Estimates are acceptable as long as they are reasonable
Mileage claims without documented evidence of journeys made cannot be verified and create a risk of inaccurate or inflated reimbursement
She should submit claims monthly rather than weekly
The company should provide a company car instead
explanation: Mileage expense claims must be supported by accurate journey records. Claims based purely on memory cannot be independently verified and are more likely to be overstated, creating a financial risk for the company and a compliance issue for the employee.

prompt: An invoice for IT equipment arrives addressed to your company, but the equipment was delivered to a residential address rather than any company office. What should you do before paying?
options: Pay it â€” IT staff sometimes work from home and receive equipment there
Pay it and note the delivery address discrepancy in your records
Hold payment and investigate internally to confirm whether the purchase was legitimately authorised and whether the delivery address is genuine
Contact the supplier to ask about the delivery address
explanation: An invoice for company equipment delivered to a residential address with no explanation is a potential sign of an employee ordering goods for personal use on the company account, or a fraudulent invoice. Investigate internally before paying.

prompt: You are told by a senior director to delete a set of invoices from the finance system because they relate to a project that has been cancelled. You are aware the invoices have already been paid. What should you do?
options: Delete the invoices as instructed since the project is cancelled
Delete the invoices but keep a personal copy
Refuse to delete paid invoices. Explain that financial records must be retained for legal and audit purposes and that the correct approach is to mark the project as closed, not to delete records
Ask the IT team to archive the invoices instead of deleting them
explanation: Deleting paid invoices from financial records is improper record-keeping and may be illegal. Financial records must be retained for the statutory period regardless of whether the related project is active. Destruction of records can constitute fraud.

prompt: You receive a call from an unknown person who says he has a copy of an overdue invoice your company has not paid. He offers to 'settle the matter quietly' if you transfer a reduced amount directly to his personal account. What should you do?
options: Transfer the reduced amount â€” it is cheaper than a legal dispute
Ask the caller for more details and call back
Do not transfer anything. Hang up, report the call to your finance manager and legal team, and check your records for any genuine outstanding debt with the claimed supplier
Ask the caller to send proof of the invoice before deciding
explanation: Callers offering to accept payment to a personal account are not representing a legitimate business. This is a fraud attempt. Report the call internally and verify any genuine outstanding debts through your own records and direct contact with the actual supplier.

prompt: Your company uses a rule that payments over Â£10,000 require authorisation from two directors. A new director wants to approve a Â£12,000 payment on her own because the other director is on holiday and it is time-sensitive. What should happen?
options: Allow the single director to approve it given the circumstances
Ask a senior finance manager to stand in as the second approver
The payment must wait until a second properly authorised director is available, or the company's escalation policy for covering absent directors must be followed
Process it as an emergency payment with retrospective approval
explanation: Dual-authorisation thresholds exist as a permanent control, not a guideline. Either the proper covering arrangement must be followed or the payment must wait. Processing high-value transactions with single authorisation because of convenience creates a significant fraud risk.

prompt: A finance team member realises she accidentally sent a spreadsheet containing all supplier bank account details to an external email address that does not belong to the intended recipient. What should she do immediately?
options: Send a follow-up email to the wrong recipient asking them to delete it
Inform her manager, raise it as a data incident, ask IT to recall the email if possible, and report it through the company's data breach process
Resend the spreadsheet to the correct recipient and move on
Change all the supplier bank details in the system to prevent misuse
explanation: Sending sensitive financial data to the wrong external recipient is a data breach. It must be reported immediately through the company's incident response process. IT may be able to recall the email, and the incident may need to be reported to relevant authorities.

prompt: An employee regularly books business travel using a personal credit card and claims reimbursement. You notice she consistently claims slightly more than the actual receipt amounts. The differences are small â€” Â£2 to Â£5 per claim. What should you do?
options: Reimburse as submitted â€” the differences are too small to matter
Reimburse the receipt amounts and note the discrepancies informally
Flag the pattern to the finance manager. A consistent pattern of small over-claims may indicate deliberate expense inflation, regardless of the amounts involved
Ask the employee to resubmit with corrected amounts on future claims only
explanation: Small but consistent discrepancies between claimed and actual amounts are not a bookkeeping error â€” they are a pattern that warrants escalation. Even minor expense fraud is fraud, and recurring behaviour must be reported and investigated.

prompt: You receive a call from someone saying he is your company's pension provider. He asks for a list of all employees who are currently enrolled, including their salaries and contribution rates. What should you do?
options: Provide the list since the pension provider legitimately needs this data
Provide the list but only with salaries, not contribution rates
Tell the caller you will call the pension provider back using the number on their official website or your existing contract to verify the request before sharing any employee data
Ask the caller to send a formal data request by post
explanation: Even if the request seems legitimate, sensitive employee financial data should never be shared with an unsolicited caller. Call back the pension provider using a verified number from your contract or their official website to confirm the request.

prompt: A new supplier submits their first invoice along with their bank details. The invoice is for Â£9,800. What should you do before setting them up and paying?
options: Set them up and pay â€” the invoice has been approved by a manager
Pay the invoice and set up the supplier record in the next billing cycle
Set up the supplier only after verifying their banking details through a call to their registered company number, and ensure a signed contract and purchase order exist before releasing any payment
Pay the invoice first and complete the supplier setup process later
explanation: New supplier onboarding must include independent verification of bank details before any payment is made. The first invoice is the highest-risk payment â€” fraudsters often intercept the setup process for new suppliers. Always verify directly with the supplier's registered contact.

prompt: During a team lunch, a finance manager tells a colleague the exact salary increase that another named employee is about to receive, before the employee has been officially notified. What did the finance manager do wrong?
options: She discussed salary information in a social setting before the employee was formally notified, breaching confidentiality
She should have sent the information by email instead of discussing it verbally
Discussing upcoming salary changes internally is standard practice and not an issue
She should only have shared the information with HR, not a colleague in finance
explanation: Salary information is confidential personal data. Sharing details of an individual's pay change before they have been formally notified â€” especially in a social setting â€” breaches confidentiality and can cause unnecessary anxiety, conflict, or distrust.

prompt: You are asked to set up a direct debit for a new service contract. The sales representative gives you the bank details over the phone and asks you to set it up right away. What is the correct approach?
options: Set up the direct debit using the details he gave over the phone
Set up the direct debit but only for the first month
Ask for the bank details in writing from the vendor's official email address or contract document, and verify the supplier's identity before setting up any direct debit
Set up the direct debit and cancel it if the first payment looks wrong
explanation: Banking details received over the phone cannot be reliably verified. Direct debits set up using unverified details could result in payments to a fraudulent account. Always obtain details in writing from an official, verified source.

prompt: An employee submits a business expense claim for a hotel stay but the receipt shows the hotel is in a different city from where the business meeting he claims to have attended took place. What should you do?
options: Approve it â€” travel plans sometimes change last minute
Approve it and ask for an explanation in the next claim cycle
Reject the claim and ask the employee to provide documentation that explains the discrepancy, including evidence of the meeting and reason for the different location
Ask a colleague to informally check whether the meeting actually happened
explanation: A receipt for accommodation in a different city from the claimed business activity is a discrepancy that requires explanation before reimbursement. Approving it without investigation could mean reimbursing personal travel expenses claimed as business.

prompt: Your company processes monthly payroll through an external payroll bureau. You receive an email from someone claiming to represent the bureau saying they need you to update the bank account details for where they send the payroll batch. What should you do?
options: Update the details since the bureau needs them to process payroll
Update the details but flag it to your payroll manager afterwards
Do not update anything. Call the payroll bureau directly using the contact number you already have on file to verify whether this request is genuine
Reply to the email asking for written confirmation on bureau letterhead
explanation: Changing the account to which a payroll batch is sent could redirect an entire month's salaries to a fraudulent account. This is an extremely high-risk change that must be verified by calling the bureau directly on a number you already hold.

prompt: A manager submits a claim for a business meal for ten people but only includes one receipt for the full amount with no list of attendees or business purpose. What should you do?
options: Process it â€” the manager is senior enough not to need itemisation
Process it but request attendee details for the next claim
Return the claim and ask the manager to provide a list of attendees and the business purpose of the meal before it can be approved
Approve up to a per-head allowance based on an assumed number of guests
explanation: Entertainment expense claims must be supported by attendee details and a clear business purpose to confirm the expense was incurred for legitimate business reasons. Without this, the claim cannot be properly verified or approved.

prompt: You receive an email asking you to approve a payment to a supplier you have never heard of for 'marketing consultancy services' in December â€” a period when your company does not usually engage external marketing. What should you do?
options: Approve it â€” the marketing team may have arranged it without notifying finance
Approve it with a note that the marketing team should be informed
Hold the payment and request confirmation from the marketing team that this supplier was engaged and that a contract or purchase order exists before approving
Ask the supplier to resend the invoice with more detail
explanation: Approving a payment to an unknown supplier without verifying that the service was actually commissioned is a control failure. Always confirm with the relevant department that the vendor was engaged, that a contract exists, and that a purchase order covers the amount.

prompt: An automated email from your finance system alerts you that your login was used at 2 a.m. last night to access the payment module, but you were asleep. What should you do immediately?
options: Log in to check what was accessed and then see if anything looks wrong
Change your password and carry on
Report the incident to IT Security immediately, do not log in to the payment module yourself, and ask IT to freeze your account and review what actions were taken overnight
Ask a colleague to check the system on your behalf while you investigate
explanation: An overnight login to a payment system that you did not perform indicates your account may be compromised. Do not log in yourself â€” this could interfere with the forensic investigation. Report to IT Security immediately so the breach can be contained and the overnight activity examined.

prompt: A colleague asks you to approve an invoice on her behalf while she is on annual leave because she is the only approver for that supplier. What should you do?
options: Approve it on her behalf since she asked you to
Approve it and add a note that she was on leave

Decline to approve on her behalf. Explain that approval must come from an authorised approver for that supplier, and raise the coverage gap with the finance manager so a proper delegation of authority is arranged
Email the supplier asking them to hold the invoice until your colleague returns
explanation: Approving an invoice on behalf of someone who is not authorised to delegate approval to you circumvents the approval control. The company should have a formal delegation-of-authority process to cover absences â€” using informal workarounds creates fraud risk.

prompt: You notice that a supplier your company has been paying for 18 months does not appear to have a website, a company registration number on their invoices, or any verifiable online presence. What should you do?
options: Continue paying as long as the services being delivered are satisfactory
Ask the supplier to create a website before the next invoice
Raise a formal query with your procurement or compliance team to verify that this supplier is a legitimately registered business before any further payments are made
Reduce future payments until the supplier can prove they are legitimate
explanation: Suppliers with no verifiable existence are a significant risk â€” they may be shell companies used to siphon funds. All suppliers should be verified as legitimate registered entities before being onboarded and payments should be frozen pending verification.

prompt: Your finance director asks you to record a payment to a vendor as a different expense category from what it actually is, so it falls under a different budget that has more headroom. What should you do?
options: Record it as directed â€” the finance director knows the budget better than you
Record it correctly but tell the finance director you have done it differently
Decline to misclassify the payment. Explain that recording it under an incorrect category misrepresents the company's actual spending and raise the concern with your compliance function if pressured
Record it in the correct category but create a manual adjustment as a workaround
explanation: Deliberately misclassifying expenses to avoid budget constraints is financial misrepresentation. It produces inaccurate financial records and can mask overspending or budget non-compliance. This must not be done regardless of who requests it.

prompt: Your company's finance system sends an email asking all users to re-enter their login details following a system update. The email contains a link to a login page hosted at 'finance-system-secure-login.net.' What should you do?
options: Enter your login details â€” system updates require re-authentication
Enter your username only to test the page
Do not enter any details. The URL is not your company's system. Report the email to IT Security and log in to the finance system only via the URL you know is correct
Forward the email to IT and wait for their guidance before doing anything
explanation: A login prompt at an unfamiliar domain is a phishing page designed to steal your credentials. Your finance system's actual URL will not change after an update. Always access systems through bookmarked, verified URLs â€” never through links in emails.

prompt: A manager in operations verbally authorises a purchase with a new supplier and tells you the paperwork will come later. The supplier calls asking when they can expect payment. What should you do?
options: Pay the supplier since a manager verbally authorised it
Ask the supplier to wait two weeks for payment
Explain to the supplier that payment cannot be processed without a formal purchase order and invoice on file, and follow up with the manager to ensure the documentation is raised promptly
Create a purchase order on the manager's behalf and process payment
explanation: Verbal authorisation is not a valid basis for payment without supporting documentation. Paying without a purchase order and invoice removes audit trail and verification controls. Prompt the manager to raise the proper documentation before any payment is released.

prompt: You receive an invoice by email and notice it has a QR code at the bottom labelled 'Scan to pay instantly.' You were going to pay via your usual bank transfer process. What should you do?
options: Scan the QR code â€” it is a faster way to pay
Scan the QR code to check where it leads, then decide
Ignore the QR code and process the payment through your company's standard verified payment method, checking the bank details on the invoice against your records first
Ask your manager whether QR code payments are allowed
explanation: QR codes on invoices can link to fraudulent payment pages or redirect funds to a different account from the one printed on the invoice. Always process payments through your company's established, secure payment method using details you have independently verified.

prompt: You receive an urgent email from the managing director asking you to approve travel and accommodation bookings for a board event totalling Â£14,000. The MD asks you not to involve the procurement team because time is short. What should you do?
options: Approve the bookings â€” the MD has the authority to bypass procurement
Approve the bookings and inform procurement afterwards
Follow the standard procurement process. Urgency is not a valid reason to exclude procurement, and any shortcuts should be escalated to the CFO rather than accepted as an instruction
Ask the MD to email procurement directly instead of you
explanation: Excluding the procurement team from a significant purchase â€” regardless of urgency â€” removes financial controls and creates fraud risk. If the urgency is genuine, the appropriate response is to engage procurement and the CFO to expedite the process, not to bypass it entirely.

prompt: You are reconciling accounts and find a credit note from a supplier that has never been applied against any invoice. It was issued eight months ago for Â£3,200. What should you do?
options: Leave it â€” it is too old to be applied now
Apply it to the next invoice from that supplier without telling anyone
Raise the unapplied credit note with your finance manager, apply it correctly against the appropriate invoice, and ensure your records are updated
Ask the supplier to reissue the credit note before applying it
explanation: Unapplied credit notes represent money owed back to the company. Leaving them unapplied means the company effectively overpays the supplier. They must be identified, applied correctly, and tracked â€” and the reason they were missed should be understood.

prompt: A contractor sends an invoice for 60 hours of work over a two-week period. You check his access logs and see he only badged into the office on four days during that period. What should you do?
options: Pay the invoice â€” contractors often work remotely
Pay it but ask the contractor to submit a timesheet next time
Hold the payment and ask the contractor to provide a detailed timesheet broken down by day, to be reconciled with your access and project records before payment is approved
Ask the contractor's supervising manager to confirm the hours informally
explanation: A significant discrepancy between claimed hours and office attendance warrants investigation. Contractors must be able to evidence the hours they bill for. Requesting a detailed timesheet and cross-referencing with project logs is standard practice before approving payment.

prompt: You are processing payroll and a new bank account number has been submitted for an employee who says she recently switched banks. The change request came by email. What should you do before updating the payroll record?
options: Update the details since the employee submitted the request themselves
Update the details and send the employee a confirmation email
Verify the request by calling the employee on their known work number before making any change to their payroll bank account details
Ask the employee to bring in a bank statement as proof and then update
explanation: Payroll account changes must be verified directly with the employee through a separate, trusted channel. Email requests alone â€” even from an employee's own address â€” can be spoofed or submitted by someone else. A quick phone verification protects the employee's salary.

prompt: You discover that a supplier your company has been paying regularly is owned by a close relative of the procurement manager who approves all their invoices. What is the issue and what should you do?
options: There is no issue unless the procurement manager is getting a kickback
The procurement manager has a financial conflict of interest that should have been declared. Report it to your compliance or ethics team immediately
Ask the procurement manager if the relationship is disclosed somewhere in their file
Continue payments since the services appear to be delivered
explanation: A company owned by a close relative of the approving manager is a conflict of interest that must be declared. If this was not disclosed, it is a serious governance failure. Report it to compliance or the ethics team â€” the manager must not approve any further invoices from that supplier.

prompt: Your company receives an invoice for printer cartridges that were apparently delivered to the main office. No one in the office recalls receiving any delivery, and there is no delivery note on file. What should you do?
options: Pay it â€” small supply invoices rarely have delivery notes
Pay it but ask the office manager to confirm receipt retroactively
Do not pay. Contact the supplier to ask for proof of delivery and confirm internally whether the goods were actually received before releasing payment
Return the invoice and ask the supplier to resubmit with a delivery note
explanation: Paying for goods you cannot confirm were delivered is a risk of both fraud and billing error. Always require proof of delivery â€” or at minimum internal confirmation that goods were received â€” before processing payment for physical goods.

prompt: At year end, your finance team is under pressure to close the books quickly. A team member suggests posting several large unverified accruals to meet the closing deadline and adjusting them properly next month. What is the risk of this approach?
options: The accruals will take longer to reverse than to get right now
Posting large unverified accruals produces inaccurate financial statements and could mislead management, investors, or auditors about the company's actual financial position
The external auditor will not notice if adjustments are made early in the next period
Unverified accruals are only a risk if they exceed the materiality threshold
explanation: Financial statements must accurately represent the company's position. Posting unverified accruals â€” even temporarily â€” produces misleading figures. If the financial statements are relied upon in that form before correction, the consequences can be serious for the business and the individuals responsible.

prompt: An employee tells you she lost her petrol receipt but she is sure she paid Â£47 for fuel for a business trip. She asks you to approve the claim based on her verbal confirmation. What should you do?
options: Approve it â€” she is a trusted employee and the amount is small
Approve half the amount as a goodwill gesture
Decline to approve a claim without a receipt. Advise her to check if her bank statement can serve as supporting evidence and follow your company's lost-receipt policy
Ask her to resubmit next month and include the receipt then
explanation: Expense claims must be supported by evidence. Most companies have a lost-receipt policy that allows alternative documentation such as a bank statement. Approving claims based solely on verbal confirmation, regardless of trust, removes the ability to verify the expense.

prompt: You receive an email that appears to come from your company's internal audit team asking you to provide a list of all payments made to one specific vendor over the past 12 months. What should you do before sharing anything?
options: Send the list immediately â€” internal audit has the right to this information
Send a summary rather than the full detail
Call the internal audit team on their known direct number to confirm the request is genuine before sharing any financial data
Ask the requestor to raise a formal information request through the audit system first
explanation: Even internal requests for financial data should be verified through a separate channel. Internal audit email addresses can be spoofed or compromised, and an informal email request is insufficient verification for releasing sensitive payment data.

prompt: A manager regularly submits expenses without receipts and becomes annoyed when asked for them. He tells you that his level of seniority means he should not need to submit receipts. What should you do?
options: Approve his expenses given his seniority to avoid conflict
Approve them this time but document that receipts were not provided

Decline to approve expenses without receipts regardless of the claimant's seniority. Expense policies apply to all staff equally. Escalate to the finance director if the manager continues to push back
Ask a more senior person in finance to make the call
explanation: Expense policies must be applied consistently regardless of seniority. Allowing senior staff to bypass receipt requirements creates inequality, undermines controls, and opens the door for fraudulent claims. Escalate rather than make exceptions.

prompt: You receive a call from someone claiming to be a supplier's accounts receivable manager. She says your company has made an overpayment and asks for your account number so she can process a refund. What should you do?
options: Give her the account number so the refund can be processed quickly
Give only the sort code and ask her to guess the account number
Do not provide any account details. Tell her you will verify any overpayment in your own records and call the supplier back using your existing contact details if a credit is due
Ask her to send the refund as a cheque instead
explanation: Callers claiming to want to issue refunds are a known vishing technique to extract banking details. Check your own records for any overpayment and â€” if one is confirmed â€” initiate the credit process by calling the supplier yourself using a number you already have.

prompt: During a busy payment run, a finance officer realises she approved a payment without checking whether a purchase order existed. The payment was for Â£7,500. What should she do?
options: Do nothing â€” the payment has gone through so it cannot be changed
Note it in her records and be more careful next time
Immediately inform her manager, investigate whether the purchase was legitimately authorised, and ensure retrospective documentation is raised or the payment is recalled if it cannot be justified
Ask the supplier to return the funds until a PO is raised
explanation: Processing a payment without a purchase order is a control failure that must be reported and investigated. If the purchase was legitimate, retrospective documentation should be raised. If it cannot be justified, the payment may need to be recalled. Staying silent is not acceptable.

prompt: A supplier asks if they can collect payment in cash this month instead of bank transfer, as they are having trouble with their account. What should you do?
options: Pay in cash â€” the supplier has a genuine need
Pay in cash but get a receipt signed by the supplier

Decline. Company payments must go through the approved payment system via bank transfer to maintain an auditable record. Cash payments to suppliers fall outside standard controls and should not be made
Agree to half in cash and half by bank transfer as a compromise
explanation: Cash payments to suppliers bypass financial controls, cannot be easily audited, and create a risk of unrecorded transactions. All supplier payments must go through the company's approved banking process regardless of the supplier's stated reason for requesting cash.

prompt: You receive an email from a named director asking you to prepare a payment schedule for the upcoming quarter and email it to an external Gmail address he provides, saying it is for a board planning session. What should you do?
options: Email the schedule to the Gmail address as requested
Send only high-level totals, not the full breakdown
Do not send financial data to a personal email address. Verify the request with the director by phone and, if genuine, share the document through your company's approved secure channel
Ask the director to forward the Gmail address request from his company email to confirm it
explanation: Sending company financial schedules to a personal Gmail account bypasses security controls and creates a data exposure risk. Even if the director is genuine, the correct process is to use an approved, secure sharing method â€” not personal email.

prompt: You receive an invoice for consultancy services rendered last month, but the description says only 'Professional Services â€” as discussed.' There is no detail of what was actually delivered. What should you do before paying?
options: Pay it â€” consultancy invoices are often vague
Pay it and ask for more detail next time
Hold payment and request a detailed breakdown of the services delivered, along with confirmation from the responsible internal manager that the work was completed satisfactorily
Ask the supplier to reword the description and resubmit
explanation: An invoice with no meaningful description of services cannot be verified. Paying without understanding what was delivered for the money makes it impossible to confirm the purchase was legitimate, complete, or value for money.

prompt: A colleague who works in finance sends you a message on a personal messaging app asking you to share the company's banking credentials so she can process a payment from home. She says she forgot to note them down before leaving the office. What should you do?
options: Send the credentials since she is a colleague and a fellow finance team member
Send only part of the credentials and let her work out the rest

Do not share banking credentials over a personal messaging app or with anyone who contacts you outside of the secure company system. Advise her to use the company's remote access solution or contact IT for assistance
Ask her to call you instead and read them out over the phone
explanation: Banking credentials should never be shared via personal messaging apps, phone calls, or any channel outside of secure company systems. The correct solution for working remotely is the company's approved remote access method â€” not sharing credentials.

prompt: A vendor phones to say that their invoice from six weeks ago has not been paid and threatens to stop supplies. When you check the system, the invoice was approved but is stuck in a payment queue with no explanation. What should you do?
options: Tell the vendor their invoice will be paid whenever the queue clears
Delete and resubmit the invoice to restart the process
Investigate why the payment is queued, release or escalate it through the correct internal process, and keep the vendor informed of a realistic payment date
Ask the vendor to resubmit a new invoice dated today
explanation: A stuck payment that has been properly approved should be investigated and resolved promptly. Deleting and restarting it creates a duplicate risk. The vendor should be kept informed with a realistic expectation â€” not left without an update.

prompt: You receive an email from a supplier with a PDF invoice attached. Before you open it, your email security system flags it with a warning that the PDF contains an embedded script. What should you do?
options: Open it anyway â€” it is from a known supplier
Open it on a different device to limit any damage
Do not open the attachment. Report it to IT Security immediately and contact the supplier through a separate channel to ask them to resend a clean version
Ask your manager to open it on your behalf
explanation: A PDF flagged for containing an embedded script is a security threat regardless of who it appears to come from. Supplier email accounts can be compromised. Report the flagged file to IT and obtain a clean copy from the supplier through a verified, separate communication channel.

prompt: You work in accounts payable and your manager asks you to keep a payment to a specific vendor off the main accounts payable ledger and record it in a separate spreadsheet she controls. What should you do?
options: Record it as instructed since your manager is responsible for the ledger
Record it in both places to be safe

Decline. All payments must be recorded in the official financial system. Maintaining off-ledger records of payments is improper accounting and may indicate an attempt to conceal transactions. Report the request to compliance
Ask the manager to explain why it needs to be off-ledger before deciding
explanation: Payments recorded outside the official financial system are hidden from auditors, management, and financial controls. This is a serious accounting irregularity that must be refused and reported through your ethics or compliance channel, regardless of your manager's seniority.

prompt: You are approving invoices and notice that a supplier's company registration number on their latest invoice is different from the one on all their previous invoices. The invoice amount is Â£11,000. What should you do?
options: Approve it â€” company registration numbers sometimes change after a restructure
Note the difference and approve the invoice
Hold the invoice and contact the supplier through your existing contact details to ask about the change in company registration number before releasing any payment
Ask the supplier to resubmit with the correct number before you process
explanation: A change in a supplier's company registration number on an invoice could indicate that a fraudulent entity has been substituted for the genuine supplier. This must be verified directly with the supplier using your existing contact details before any payment is released.

prompt: A finance manager asks a team member to pre-sign several blank cheques before going on annual leave 'in case any payments need to be made while she is away.' What did the finance manager do wrong?
options: She should have signed the cheques in the presence of a witness
She left pre-signed blank cheques, which could be used to process any amount to any payee without her knowledge or authorisation
She should have asked a director to sign instead
She did not leave any instructions with the team member about when to use the cheques
explanation: Pre-signing blank cheques removes all control over the amount and payee, effectively giving whoever holds them unlimited access to company funds. This is a serious financial control failure. Proper absence coverage should involve authorised delegation, not pre-signed instruments.

prompt: You are on a call with a supplier's representative who suddenly asks for your company's VAT registration number and bank sort code, saying they need it to process a credit. You have not requested any credit. What should you do?
options: Provide both details since it is just administrative information
Give the VAT number but not the sort code
Tell the caller you have not requested a credit and will not provide any company financial details during an unsolicited call. End the call and report it to your finance manager
Ask the caller to email the request so you have it in writing
explanation: Unsolicited requests for financial identifiers such as VAT numbers and sort codes during a call you did not initiate are a data harvesting tactic. End the call and report it. If a genuine credit is due, it will be raised through a verifiable process.

prompt: A member of the finance team leaves the company and her replacement asks if he can use her login to access historical payment records while his own account is being set up. What should happen instead?
options: Let him use her login temporarily since it is just for viewing records
Change her password and give him the new one for a limited time
Disable the former employee's account immediately and arrange for IT to set up the new employee's account with the correct access permissions before he begins working in the system
Ask the new employee to work with a colleague until his account is ready
explanation: Former employee accounts must be deactivated immediately upon departure. Sharing or reusing those credentials is a policy and security violation. A new employee should have their own account configured before they begin accessing financial systems.

prompt: You receive an invoice from a supplier in a currency different from the one agreed in your contract. The supplier says their pricing has changed. What should you do?
options: Pay in the new currency since exchange rates fluctuate
Pay in the contracted currency and ignore the new invoice
Hold the payment and clarify with the supplier whether the contract has been formally amended to change the invoicing currency before processing payment in any currency
Pay in whichever currency is cheaper at today's exchange rate
explanation: Invoicing in a different currency from what was contracted may be a billing error or a deliberate attempt to extract more money. The contract terms govern the payment, and any change must be formally agreed and documented before the new terms apply.

prompt: You are about to release a large batch payment when you notice the payment file was prepared by the same person who also approved it. Your company's policy requires these to be two different people. What should you do?
options: Release the batch â€” both steps were done within the finance team
Release it this time since the approver is senior enough to cover both roles
Do not release the batch. Escalate to your finance manager to arrange for a proper independent review and approval before the payment is released
Release it but document that the dual-control requirement was not met
explanation: Dual-control requirements exist so that no single person can unilaterally prepare and authorise a payment. When this control is not followed, even for legitimate payments, it must be corrected before release â€” not released and documented as a known exception.

prompt: Your accounts team receives a credit note from a supplier reducing the amount owed by Â£5,000. You cannot find any corresponding return or disputed invoice in your records. What should you do?
options: Apply the credit note â€” any credit is beneficial to the company
Apply half and query the rest
Do not apply the credit note until you have contacted the supplier to understand what it relates to and confirmed it is legitimate and accurately calculated
Ask the supplier to cancel the credit note and reissue it with a description
explanation: Applying an unexplained credit note without understanding what it relates to could result in under-payment to the supplier, or it may be a sign of an error. All credit notes must be matched to a specific transaction or agreed adjustment before being applied.

prompt: An invoice arrives addressed to your company for Â£3,400 worth of office furniture. Your office manager confirms no furniture was ordered and no delivery was received. What should you do?
options: Pay it in case someone else in the company ordered it without telling you
Hold the payment and investigate internally to confirm whether anyone in the organisation placed this order, then reject the invoice if no one did
Contact the supplier to ask them to collect the furniture
Pay half and dispute the rest
explanation: Invoices for goods or services your company has no record of ordering should never be paid without investigation. This could be a billing error, a fraudulent invoice, or a sign that an employee has made an unauthorised purchase. Investigate before paying anything.

prompt: Your company's finance system flags an unusual login from a foreign country on the account of a finance team member who is currently sitting in your UK office. What should happen immediately?
options: Tell the team member and ask her to change her password when she gets a chance
Disable the team member's account immediately, investigate the source of the foreign login, and treat this as a potential account compromise requiring urgent IT Security involvement
Log the alert and monitor for further unusual activity over the next few days
Ask the team member if she knows anyone abroad who might have used her account
explanation: A simultaneous login from a foreign location while the account holder is present in the UK indicates the account credentials have been stolen. The account must be disabled immediately to prevent further unauthorised access to financial systems.

prompt: A supplier emails to say they are offering a 5% early payment discount if you pay their invoice today instead of on the standard 30-day terms. The payment would need to go to a different account than the one on the invoice. What should you do?
options: Take the discount and pay to the new account to save money
Pay to the invoice account at the standard terms and ignore the offer
