Do not pay to the new account based on this email alone. Call the supplier on your existing contact number to verify the discount offer and confirm which account to use before making any payment
Ask your manager whether the discount is worth the risk
explanation: Early payment discounts are sometimes used as a lure to divert payments to a fraudulent account. Never redirect a payment to a different account based on an email alone. Verify with the supplier directly using your existing contact details.

prompt: You are processing the monthly supplier payment run and your colleague asks you to add a personal bank transfer to a friend of hers into the batch, saying she will reimburse the company on payday. What should you do?
options: Add it since she has promised to pay it back
Add it but keep a note to remind her to reimburse

Decline. Company payment systems must only be used for authorised business payments. Using them for personal transfers â€” even temporarily â€” is a misuse of company funds and a serious breach of financial controls
Ask your manager if it is allowed as a one-off
explanation: Processing personal transfers through company payment systems is misuse of company funds regardless of the intent to repay. It creates unauthorised transactions, distorts financial records, and may expose both the employee and the company to legal liability.

prompt: A caller contacts the IT helpdesk saying he is the sales director and needs his password reset urgently before a client presentation in 20 minutes. He sounds stressed and gives the director's name and department. What should the helpdesk agent do?
options: Reset the password immediately â€” the presentation is time-critical
Reset it and ask him to change it again after the meeting
Follow the standard identity verification process before resetting any password, regardless of urgency or the caller's stated seniority
Ask the caller to call back in an hour when things are less busy
explanation: Urgency and seniority are the two most common pressure tactics used to bypass identity checks. A helpdesk agent must follow the verification process for every caller â€” knowing someone's name and department is not sufficient identity proof.

prompt: An employee's manager calls the IT helpdesk and asks for the employee's temporary login credentials to be sent to the manager's email, saying the employee is off sick and the manager needs access to finish a project. What should the helpdesk agent do?
options: Send the credentials to the manager â€” he has legitimate authority over the employee's work
Send a read-only token to the manager instead of full credentials

Decline. Sharing another employee's credentials â€” even with their manager â€” is a policy violation. Offer to help the manager access only the specific files needed through an approved data-access process
Reset the sick employee's password and give the new one to the manager
explanation: Managers do not have the right to access an employee's personal login credentials. Each account is individual. If business-critical files are needed, IT can arrange access through a controlled process â€” not by sharing credentials.

prompt: A woman arrives at the server room door and says she is from a third-party IT maintenance company here to perform scheduled maintenance. She does not have an access badge but shows a company-branded lanyard. What should the security officer do?
options: Let her in â€” the lanyard looks official
Let her in but escort her at all times
Ask her to wait outside and verify her visit by contacting the internal IT manager who should have pre-authorised the maintenance before allowing any access
Check her ID card and then let her in
explanation: Branded lanyards can be purchased or faked. Third-party maintenance visits must be pre-approved and registered, and access should only be granted after confirmation from the internal contact who arranged the visit â€” not based on appearance alone.

prompt: A helpdesk agent receives an email from what looks like the head of HR asking him to create a new admin-level account in the HR system for a new starter who begins on Monday. What should he do?
options: Create the account immediately â€” HR has authority to request this
Create the account but set it to expire after one month
Verify the request by calling the head of HR on a known number and ensure the new starter's role genuinely requires admin-level access before creating the account
Create a standard account and upgrade it to admin once the person starts
explanation: Admin-level accounts carry high risk and must be created only after verifying both the requester's identity and whether the level of access is genuinely required for the role. An email alone â€” even from HR â€” is insufficient authorisation.

prompt: An employee is terminated on a Friday afternoon. The HR manager tells the IT helpdesk to disable the employee's accounts first thing Monday morning. What is wrong with this instruction?
options: Account disabling should be done by the employee's line manager, not IT
The employee's accounts should have been disabled at the time of termination on Friday, not two business days later
Account disabling requires a minimum notice period of 24 hours
IT should archive the accounts rather than disable them
explanation: Accounts belonging to terminated employees must be disabled at the moment of termination â€” not days later. Leaving accounts active over a weekend gives the former employee continued access to company systems, data, and email.

prompt: A caller to the IT helpdesk says she has forgotten her username as well as her password and asks the agent to look both up and read them out. What should the helpdesk agent do?
options: Read out the username since that is not sensitive, then reset the password
Read out both â€” the caller just needs to get back to work
Verify the caller's identity through the approved process, provide the username if found, and send a password reset link to the employee's registered recovery contact â€” not read any password aloud
Tell the caller to ask their manager for the information instead
explanation: Even usernames can help an attacker if paired with other information. Passwords should never be read out by anyone. The correct process is identity verification, then a secure self-service reset â€” not verbal disclosure of credentials.

prompt: An operations manager notices that a former employee's access card was handed in when they left, but no one informed IT to revoke the employee's remote access to the operations scheduling system. What should the operations manager do immediately?
options: Email IT to cancel the access when they get a chance
Assume the former employee will not misuse access they no longer need
Contact IT Security immediately to revoke the remote access without delay, and review whether the former employee has logged in since their departure
Wait to see if the employee tries to log in before revoking access
explanation: Physical badge return does not automatically revoke digital system access. All access â€” physical and digital â€” must be revoked at the time of departure. Any delay leaves the door open for a disgruntled or dishonest former employee to access company systems.

prompt: A helpdesk agent is on a call with someone who correctly answers the security questions used to verify identity. However, the agent notices the caller's voice sounds different from the last time they spoke with this employee. What should the agent do?
options: Proceed â€” the security questions were answered correctly
Ask one more security question to be safe, then proceed

Follow the process as designed â€” if the verification questions are answered correctly, proceed. If genuinely concerned, escalate to a senior agent to apply additional verification steps before taking action
Reset the password and flag it to the security team afterwards
explanation: Verification processes are the defined safeguard. If the agent has genuine concerns beyond a voice difference, the correct response is to escalate to a senior colleague for additional verification â€” not to proceed and report afterwards.

prompt: Payroll has just printed a batch of employee payslips for distribution. A member of the payroll team leaves the entire printed batch on a meeting room table while she goes to lunch. What did she do wrong?
options: She should have printed them in a smaller batch
She left sensitive payroll documents containing personal salary information unattended in a shared space accessible to all staff
She used the wrong printer setting for confidential documents
She should have waited until after lunch to print them
explanation: Printed payslips contain sensitive personal financial data. Leaving them unattended in a shared area allows anyone to read, photograph, or take them. Sensitive documents must never be left unattended in communal spaces.

prompt: An employee swipes his access badge to enter a secure area, then holds the door open for three colleagues behind him without each of them swiping their own badges. What is the security problem here?
options: The door should have closed faster after the first swipe
Allowing multiple people to enter on one badge swipe means some individuals enter without their access being recorded or verified
Only one badge swipe is needed if staff are entering together
The colleagues should have signed a visitor log instead
explanation: Tailgating defeats the purpose of access control. Each individual must swipe their own badge so that access is recorded and only authorised individuals enter. Tailgating also means you cannot verify who is in a secure area at any time.

prompt: An HR coordinator is disposing of printed job applications that were not shortlisted. She puts them in the general office bin near her desk. What should she have done instead?
options: Shredded them or placed them in a confidential waste bin, as job applications contain personal data that must be securely destroyed
Emailed the candidates to ask permission to dispose of their applications
Kept them for twelve months before disposal
Put them in a sealed envelope in the recycling bin
explanation: Job applications contain personal data including names, addresses, and employment history. They must be disposed of securely using a shredder or certified confidential waste service â€” not placed in an ordinary bin where the contents remain readable.

prompt: A caller to IT support says he is a new employee who started today and needs his laptop set up. He does not appear on the active employee list the agent pulls up. What should the agent do?
options: Set up the laptop anyway â€” HR sometimes delays adding people to the system
Ask the caller to email from his work account to prove he works there
Do not proceed. Tell the caller you are unable to set up accounts for individuals who do not appear on the verified employee list, and ask him to contact HR to resolve the discrepancy first
Take the caller's personal details and add him to the list manually
explanation: Setting up accounts for people who are not on the verified employee list risks creating access for someone with no legitimate entitlement. The agent must insist on a verified record before proceeding.

prompt: During an office move, a box of HR files including signed employment contracts and performance review documents is left unlabelled in the corridor for two days. What is the problem?
options: Unlabelled boxes make unpacking harder
Sensitive HR documents were left accessible in an unsecured corridor, creating a risk of unauthorised access, loss, or damage
The files should have been scanned before being moved
Files should not be moved during business hours
explanation: Sensitive documents must be kept secure at all times â€” including during an office move. They should be in clearly labelled, locked containers and never left accessible in shared or public areas.

prompt: A helpdesk agent resets an employee's password and reads the temporary password aloud to the caller during a recorded call. What is wrong with what the agent did?
options: The agent should have used a stronger temporary password
Reading a password aloud during a recorded call means the temporary password is stored in the recording and could be accessed by anyone who reviews it
Temporary passwords do not need to be kept secret
The agent should have emailed the temporary password instead of calling
explanation: Passwords â€” even temporary ones â€” should never be read aloud during recorded calls. Call recordings can be accessed by multiple people. The correct process is to send a password reset link to a pre-registered, verified recovery contact.

prompt: A member of the operations team needs to enter the server room to retrieve a piece of equipment. He has a valid access card but the server room requires two-person access for security purposes. His colleague has gone home. What should he do?
options: Enter alone since he has a valid access card and a legitimate reason
Ask any passing colleague to accompany him temporarily
Follow the two-person access policy and contact the on-call manager to arrange proper access with an authorised second person, rather than entering alone
Wait until the next day when his colleague returns
explanation: Two-person access rules exist to prevent any individual from accessing sensitive areas without a witness. Entering alone â€” even for a legitimate reason â€” violates this control. The right response is to follow the escalation process, not improvise a workaround.

prompt: The HR team receives a request to update an employee's home address and next-of-kin information via an email that appears to come from the employee. What should HR do before making the change?
options: Make the update immediately â€” the employee is entitled to update their own details
Make the update and send a confirmation email to the address on file
Verify the request by contacting the employee through a previously verified channel such as a call to their work phone before changing any personal details
Ask the employee to submit the change request through the self-service portal instead
explanation: Personal detail updates â€” especially home address â€” can be used to redirect sensitive HR documents. An employee's email account may be accessed by someone else. Always verify through a separate, previously confirmed channel before making changes.

prompt: A former employee returns to the office three weeks after leaving to collect personal belongings. A colleague notices the former employee is walking around the open-plan floor and looking at a colleague's screen. What should the colleague do?
options: Assume the visit is innocent since the person is known to everyone
Politely alert a manager or security that the former employee is in the working area without escort, and ensure they are accompanied back to reception
Ask the former employee to leave by themselves
Send an email to HR after the former employee has left
explanation: Former employees who return to the premises have no authorised access to working areas. They should be escorted at all times and restricted to the area relevant to their stated purpose. Alert security or management promptly.

prompt: A member of staff from another department calls the IT helpdesk asking for access to a shared drive belonging to the finance team. She says her manager told her verbally that she should have access. What should the helpdesk agent do?
options: Grant the access since her manager approved it
Grant view-only access as a compromise
Ask the caller to have her manager submit a formal access request through the proper approval process before any access is granted
Check if any other team member has similar access and grant the same level
explanation: Access to sensitive shared drives must be granted through a documented, approved process â€” not based on verbal approvals relayed by a caller. Granting access without proper authorisation bypasses access controls and creates unaccountable data exposure.

prompt: An operations supervisor finds that three members of her team all share the same login to the warehouse management system because it is easier than using individual accounts. What is the problem?
options: The system may not handle multiple simultaneous users well
Shared logins make it impossible to identify which individual performed which action, removing accountability and making it harder to detect errors or misconduct
The team should use separate systems for each shift
Shared logins are fine as long as the password is changed regularly
explanation: Individual accountability is a fundamental security and audit principle. When multiple people share one login, it is impossible to trace who performed which action â€” a critical problem if an error, fraud, or incident needs to be investigated.

prompt: A new employee has been set up with a system account that gives her access to every department's data because the IT team copied the permissions from a long-serving employee who has accumulated access over many years. What went wrong?
options: The IT team used the wrong account as a template
The new employee was given excessive access rights that do not reflect her actual role, because copying an experienced employee's permissions carries over all their historically accumulated access
The new employee should have been consulted about what access she needs
This is standard practice and nothing went wrong
explanation: Copying permissions from an existing employee is a common but flawed shortcut. Long-serving employees often accumulate far more access than their role requires. New accounts should be provisioned based solely on the role's current access needs.

prompt: An HR manager is emailing a recruitment agency a list of shortlisted candidates' CVs. She accidentally attaches the salary review spreadsheet for the entire company. She notices immediately after sending. What should she do?
options: Send a follow-up email asking the agency to ignore the attachment
Immediately notify her manager, contact the recruitment agency to request deletion of the email, and report it as a data breach through the company's incident process
Recall the email through her email client and hope it worked
Wait to see if the agency mentions it before deciding whether to report it
explanation: Sending salary data for all staff to an external recruitment agency is a data breach. Attempting to recall may help but is not reliable. The incident must be reported through the company's formal data breach process without delay.

prompt: A visitor to the office claims she has a meeting with a department head and asks the receptionist to print a document from her personal USB drive because her laptop battery is dead. What should the receptionist do?
options: Plug in the USB and print the document â€” it is a simple favour
Plug it in but scan it first before printing
Decline. Company computers must not be used with unknown external USB devices. Offer the visitor alternative solutions such as a guest Wi-Fi connection to a web printing service
Call IT first and if they say it is okay, plug in the USB
explanation: Plugging unknown USB devices into company computers is a serious security risk. Even a brief connection can introduce software that compromises the device. Offer alternatives that do not involve connecting the USB to a company machine.

prompt: An employee in the IT helpdesk is approached in person by a colleague asking for his own password to be reset without going through the normal ticketing system, as a personal favour. The helpdesk employee agrees and resets it verbally. What did he do wrong?
options: He should have asked the colleague to wait in a queue
He bypassed the standard ticketing and verification process, meaning the reset was not logged and the colleague's identity was not formally verified before the change was made
He reset a password outside of business hours
He should have involved a second helpdesk agent
explanation: All helpdesk actions â€” including password resets â€” must go through the official process. Informal resets create unaudited changes, bypass identity verification, and set a precedent that controls can be skipped for people you know.

prompt: During an HR investigation into an employee conduct matter, the HR officer discusses the details of the case openly in the office kitchen with another HR colleague while several other staff are present. What did the HR officer do wrong?
options: She discussed an HR investigation in a non-private space, potentially breaching the confidentiality of the person under investigation and compromising the integrity of the process
She should not have involved a second HR colleague
HR officers are allowed to discuss cases openly within the HR team
She should have waited until the investigation was concluded before discussing it
explanation: Active HR investigations are strictly confidential. Discussing case details in a shared space risks being overheard, can bias the investigation, and breaches the employee's right to a fair and private process. Such discussions must happen in a private, secured environment.

prompt: A helpdesk agent is helping a user over the phone and asks her to read out the one-time code sent to her mobile phone as part of multi-factor authentication. The user reads it out and the agent enters it. What is wrong with this approach?
options: The agent should have waited for the code to be sent to email instead

The agent should not be entering authentication codes on behalf of users â€” this undermines the security that multi-factor authentication is designed to provide and could be abused to access accounts without consent
One-time codes expire too quickly to be useful over the phone
The agent should have asked for a different type of code
explanation: Multi-factor authentication is designed to verify that the account's legitimate owner is the one logging in. If an agent can collect and enter MFA codes on behalf of users, that protection is bypassed â€” an attacker impersonating a helpdesk agent could use the same technique.

prompt: An operations team leader finds that a member of her team has been taking photos of the production schedule â€” which contains client order volumes and delivery timings â€” on his personal mobile phone. He says it is for his own reference. What should she do?
options: Allow it if he promises to delete the photos when no longer needed
Remind him to keep the photos private
Tell him to delete the photos immediately and remind him that photographing operational data containing client information on personal devices is not permitted without explicit authorisation
Report it to IT and wait for their guidance
explanation: Photographing sensitive operational or client data with a personal device transfers company data outside of secure, controlled systems. This breaches data handling policy and creates a risk of accidental or deliberate data exposure. The photos must be deleted immediately.

prompt: A caller contacts the IT helpdesk saying they need a password reset for a specific user account because they are covering for that person while they are on leave. What should the helpdesk agent do?
options: Reset the password and send it to the caller since they are covering
Reset it but only give them a limited-time password

Decline. Only the account holder can request a reset of their own credentials. If access is needed during leave, it must be arranged through a formal delegation process â€” not by resetting someone else's password
Ask the user's manager to authorise the reset by email and then proceed
explanation: Password resets must only be initiated by or for the account holder through the verified identity process. Shared access during someone's absence must be handled through formal delegation â€” not by giving a colleague access to another person's account.

prompt: An HR assistant prints out the list of all staff due for redundancy as part of a restructure process. She leaves the printout face-up on her desk while she attends a meeting. What did she do wrong?
options: She printed the document without her manager's permission
She left a highly sensitive list of named employees facing redundancy visible to anyone passing her desk, risking premature and unauthorised disclosure
She should have kept the document in a locked folder on her computer rather than printing it
She printed too many copies of the document
explanation: Redundancy lists are among the most sensitive HR documents. Leaving them visible on a desk could devastate employee morale, trigger grievances, and breach the confidentiality owed to those individuals. Sensitive documents must always be secured when not in hand.

prompt: An IT helpdesk agent successfully verifies a caller's identity and resets their password. The caller then asks the agent to also grant them access to a new shared folder while they are already on the phone. What should the agent do?
options: Grant the folder access since the caller has already been verified
Grant view-only access to the folder as a reasonable compromise

Treat the folder access as a separate request that must go through the proper authorisation process â€” identity verification for a password reset does not automatically authorise all other requests made during the same call
Check whether the folder contains sensitive data before deciding
explanation: Each request must be independently authorised. Verifying someone for a password reset does not grant them a blank authorisation for all subsequent requests made in the same call. Folder access requires its own approval process.

prompt: An employee's access badge is reported as lost. Two days later, it has still not been deactivated by the security team because no one filed the paperwork. What is the risk of this delay?
options: The employee cannot get into the building until a new badge is issued
A lost badge that remains active can be used by anyone who finds or stole it to access secured areas of the building, with no indication that the entry is unauthorised
The employee may be fined for losing their badge
The badge may be demagnetised by the time it is found
explanation: A lost or stolen access badge must be deactivated immediately â€” not days later. An active badge that is not in the employee's possession is an open door for anyone who has it to enter secured areas of the premises.

prompt: A caller to the IT helpdesk says he is calling on behalf of his team and needs the helpdesk to reset the passwords for six team members at once. He provides all six employee names and says they are all locked out. What should the agent do?
options: Reset all six passwords and email them to the caller
Reset two as a test and ask the others to call in individually if needed
Decline to reset multiple accounts on behalf of a single caller. Each affected employee must call individually and pass the identity verification process before their own password is reset
Ask the caller to send an email listing all six names and then process the resets
explanation: Resetting multiple accounts based on one caller's say-so bypasses the individual verification that protects each of those accounts. An attacker who knows a team structure could use this to gain access to multiple accounts in one call.

prompt: An operations manager finds that a maintenance engineer has been given a permanent access badge to the warehouse rather than a temporary visitor badge for the duration of the maintenance contract. What should happen?
options: Keep the permanent badge since the contract may be extended
The permanent badge should be replaced with temporary, time-limited access for the duration of the contract and revoked when the contract ends
Ask the engineer to sign a security agreement and keep the permanent badge
Issue a second temporary badge and collect the permanent one next week
explanation: Contractors and temporary workers should only have access for the duration of their engagement, issued as time-limited credentials. Permanent badges remove the automatic expiry safeguard and are often forgotten about when the contract ends.

prompt: An HR team member is working from home and prints company HR documents on her home printer. She then leaves the printed documents on her home desk when her child has friends visiting. What is the problem?
options: Home printers are less reliable than office printers
Sensitive HR documents were left visible in a non-secure home environment where people outside the company could see them
She did not get permission from her manager to print at home
She should have used encrypted print settings on the home printer
explanation: Working from home does not reduce the obligation to keep company documents secure. Sensitive printed documents must be kept out of sight of anyone who does not have authorisation to see them, including family members and visitors.

prompt: An IT helpdesk ticket is raised to grant a new employee access to the payroll system with the note that the employee will need access to everything eventually. What should the helpdesk agent do?
options: Grant full access now to save time later
Grant read-only access as a starting point
Request clarification on the specific access required for the employee's role right now, and grant only what is necessary â€” not broad access in anticipation of future needs
Escalate to a senior agent who can decide the appropriate access level
explanation: Access must be provisioned based on current role requirements, not anticipated future needs. Granting broad access now means the employee has more access than their role requires, increasing risk if their account is ever compromised.

prompt: A security guard notices that the door to the network communications room has been propped open with a chair. No maintenance or IT work is scheduled for today. What should the guard do?
options: Remove the chair and close the door â€” problem solved
Remove the chair, close and lock the door, then report the incident to IT Security and investigate how long the door has been open and whether anyone entered
Leave a note asking staff not to prop the door open
Call the IT manager to ask if they left it open
explanation: A propped-open door to a secure network room is a physical security incident. The immediate response is to secure the door, but the incident must also be reported and investigated â€” the door may have been opened deliberately to allow tampering with equipment inside.

prompt: An HR manager is conducting an exit interview with a departing employee. The employee mentions she has already copied several company HR templates to her personal laptop to use in her next job. What should the HR manager do?
options: Tell her not to use them and move on with the exit interview
Ask her to return the files to the company and ensure IT is notified to investigate what was copied and whether any other company data was transferred
Remind her the templates are copyrighted and she should not use them
Note it in the exit interview report for future reference
explanation: Copying company documents to personal devices without authorisation is a data breach, regardless of whether the files seem harmless. IT must be notified to investigate the extent of data copied, and the company may need to take further steps to recover or secure the data.

prompt: A caller contacts the IT helpdesk and says they are a contractor working on a project for the IT director. They need an account creating immediately and say the IT director will confirm later. What should the agent do?
options: Create the account and follow up with the IT director afterwards
Create a temporary account that expires in 24 hours

Decline to create any account without prior authorisation from the IT director or the official project sponsor. Ask the caller to have the IT director submit the request through the proper process first
Ask the caller to email the IT director and CC the helpdesk before creating the account
explanation: Accounts must be created based on pre-existing, documented authorisation â€” not on the promise that confirmation will come later. Retroactive confirmation is a known social engineering tactic. Create accounts after authorisation, not before.

prompt: An employee notices that a colleague's access badge â€” belonging to someone who left the company six months ago â€” is still attached to a lanyard hanging on a hook in the office kitchen. What should she do?
options: Leave it â€” it has probably already been deactivated
Take it to the security desk so it can be checked and deactivated if still active, and report the finding to her manager
Hand it back to the colleague's former line manager
Put it in a drawer so it is not visible
explanation: A former employee's badge that was not returned or deactivated represents a potential security risk. It should be handed to security immediately for deactivation checks, and the lapse in the offboarding process should be reported so it can be corrected.

prompt: An IT helpdesk agent receives a call from someone who says they are an employee's spouse and needs to know the employee's work email address because the employee has been in an accident and is hospitalised. What should the agent do?
options: Provide the email address since it is an emergency
Provide the first name only and let the caller work out the rest
Express concern but explain that employee contact information cannot be shared with external callers. Direct the caller to the company's HR emergency contact line or main switchboard
Ask the caller to provide proof of the accident before sharing anything
explanation: Employee contact details are personal data. Sharing them with an unverified external caller â€” even in an apparent emergency â€” could be a social engineering attempt. The correct response is to direct the caller to HR or the main switchboard who have proper protocols for genuine emergencies.

prompt: An operations team is issued with shared tablet devices for scanning deliveries. One tablet is discovered missing at the end of a shift and no one knows when it was last seen. What should the operations supervisor do immediately?
options: Wait until the next shift and see if it turns up
Report the missing device to IT Security immediately so it can be remotely locked or wiped, and begin an investigation into when and where it was last used
Check all desk drawers and leave a note on the notice board
File a report at the end of the week during the regular team meeting
explanation: A missing company device must be reported to IT Security without delay so it can be remotely locked or wiped before any data on it is accessed. Every hour of delay increases the risk of data exposure.

prompt: An employee calls IT to report that she received an MFA prompt on her phone that she did not initiate â€” someone is attempting to log in to her account. The IT helpdesk agent tells her to call back in the morning when a senior agent is available. What did the agent do wrong?
options: The agent should have asked her to approve the prompt to confirm who is trying to log in
The agent failed to treat an active, in-progress account compromise attempt as an urgent security incident requiring immediate escalation and account suspension
The agent should have offered to reset her password over the phone
MFA prompts that a user did not initiate are not worth acting on immediately
explanation: An uninitiated MFA prompt means someone is actively trying to break into the account right now. This is an urgent security incident. The account should be suspended immediately and the incident escalated â€” telling the caller to wait until morning is a critical failure.

prompt: HR is distributing updated employment contracts to staff. One manager takes a stack of contracts for his entire team and says he will hand them out himself. Two weeks later, three employees say they never received their contracts. What went wrong?
options: The contracts were printed on the wrong paper

Distributing sensitive personal documents through a third party with no tracking or confirmation created a gap where documents were unaccounted for, leaving staff without their contracts and creating a potential confidentiality risk
The manager should have signed the contracts before distributing them
Contracts should always be sent by post, not handed out in person
explanation: Sensitive personal documents like contracts should be distributed directly to each individual with a record of receipt. Delegating distribution through a manager with no audit trail creates risk of loss, delay, and potential exposure of one employee's details to another.

prompt: A helpdesk agent is working on a support ticket that requires viewing an employee's personal account settings. He shares his screen with a colleague to ask for help and the employee's personal details are visible to a small group in the open office. What should he have done instead?
options: Covered the screen with his hand while sharing
Moved to a private area or used a privacy screen before displaying another person's personal account details, rather than doing so in an open shared space
Asked the colleague to sign a confidentiality agreement first
Helped the employee at a different time when fewer people are around
explanation: Personal account information must be handled with discretion. Displaying it in an open office â€” even briefly for a colleague's help â€” risks exposure to bystanders. IT staff should use private spaces or appropriate screen controls when handling personal data.

prompt: An operations manager is leaving the company and hands his building access badge to his successor on his last day, telling her it will save time while she waits for her own badge to be processed. What should happen instead?
options: The successor can use the badge for a few days while hers is sorted
The outgoing manager must return his badge to security upon departure, and the new manager must go through the proper badge issuance process before being granted building access
The badge should be taped over with a new name label for the successor
HR should hold the badge until the new manager's official start date
explanation: Access badges are non-transferable and must be surrendered upon departure. The successor should receive their own badge through the proper process. Using a former employee's badge means entry is logged against a person who no longer works there, breaking the audit trail.

prompt: An employee in the IT team has administrator-level access to the HR system from a project that ended eight months ago. He still uses this access occasionally to help HR colleagues with queries informally. What is the issue?
options: He should be charging HR for his time

He has retained elevated access well beyond the project's end date and is using it informally without authorisation â€” this is both an access control failure and a risk if his account is ever compromised
He should have asked IT to extend the access formally
Helping colleagues with system queries is an appropriate use of existing access
explanation: Access should be revoked when the reason for it ends. Retained access that is used informally â€” even helpfully â€” is uncontrolled and unaudited. It also means the organisation does not have an accurate picture of who has elevated access to sensitive systems.

prompt: A team member raises a helpdesk ticket saying she is unable to access her email. When the IT agent investigates, he finds the account has already been accessed from two different countries in the past hour. What should the agent do?
options: Reset her password and send her a new one so she can get back in
Tell her to wait while he investigates and do nothing until he has a full picture

Immediately suspend the account, escalate to IT Security as a confirmed compromise incident, and contact the employee through an alternative verified channel to inform her and begin the response process
Change the password and ask the employee to set up MFA before logging back in
explanation: Login activity from two different countries simultaneously is a confirmed sign of account compromise. The account must be suspended immediately to stop the active breach, and the incident must be escalated â€” not simply resolved with a password reset.

prompt: An employee working in the HR team posts a photo on her personal Instagram from the office, captioning it 'busy week â€” so many redundancies to process.' What did she do wrong?
options: She posted during work hours
She publicly disclosed confidential operational HR information on social media, which could alarm employees, breach confidentiality, and cause significant harm to those affected
She included identifiable colleagues in the photo without their consent
She posted from a personal account rather than the company's official account
explanation: Sharing information about confidential HR processes â€” even casually on personal social media â€” is a serious breach. Redundancy processes are strictly confidential to protect those affected. This could cause significant distress, trigger legal issues, and violate data protection obligations.

prompt: An IT helpdesk agent finishes a support call and realises he forgot to close the employee's account settings page on his screen. He leaves his desk for a team meeting without locking his computer. What is the risk?
options: The computer may overheat if left on
Any person passing the desk can see the employee's personal account settings on an unlocked screen, breaching that employee's privacy and potentially exposing sensitive account information
The session will time out automatically so there is no risk
The screen saver will activate and hide the information quickly
explanation: IT staff handling personal account data have the same clean-screen obligation as all other employees. Leaving a screen unlocked with another person's account visible is a privacy breach. Always lock the screen before leaving your desk.

prompt: A caller to the IT helpdesk correctly answers the security question but then says they do not want the password reset link sent to their registered mobile number â€” they want it sent to a different email address they provide. What should the agent do?
options: Send the link to the new email address since the caller has already verified their identity
Send to both addresses so the employee definitely receives it
Decline to send the reset link to an unregistered address. The reset must be sent to the pre-registered recovery contact on file to ensure it reaches the genuine account holder
Ask the caller to update their registered contact details first and then reset
explanation: Sending a reset link to an unregistered address defeats the security purpose of the recovery process â€” it may send access to an attacker who has guessed the security question. Reset links must only go to pre-registered, verified recovery contacts.

prompt: An operations supervisor notices that a member of her team consistently stays in the building an hour after his shift ends and has been seen near the server room on CCTV. He is not an IT staff member. What should the supervisor do?
options: Ask the employee why he is staying late as a friendly conversation

Report the observed pattern to IT Security and physical security so they can review the CCTV, check server room access logs, and investigate whether there is a legitimate reason for his presence near that area
Remind all staff that the server room is restricted
Monitor the situation for another week before deciding whether to report it
explanation: Unusual patterns of behaviour near sensitive areas â€” especially from non-IT staff â€” warrant investigation by security teams. Handling it as a friendly conversation may alert the individual without properly investigating. Prompt reporting allows a review of access logs and CCTV.

prompt: An HR manager is interviewing a candidate in a meeting room that has a glass wall facing the main office. Several colleagues glance in and can read the candidate's CV on the table. What should the HR manager have done?
options: Turned the CV face down during the interview
Chosen a private meeting room without a glass wall or used a privacy screen, and kept the candidate's documents face down when not being actively reviewed
Asked colleagues not to look through the glass
Conducted the interview with the candidate facing away from the glass
explanation: Candidate information is personal data that must be kept confidential during interviews. Conducting an interview in a room where documents are visible to passers-by is a privacy risk. Private, appropriately screened spaces should be used for all sensitive discussions.

prompt: A member of the IT team is troubleshooting an employee's laptop remotely and sees a personal banking website open in the browser. The IT agent takes a screenshot of the full screen for their support log. What did the agent do wrong?
options: Screenshots are needed for support logs so this is acceptable
The agent captured and stored an image containing the employee's personal banking information, which is sensitive personal data that should never be included in a support log
The agent should have asked the employee to close the browser first
The agent should have used a different logging method
explanation: Support screenshots must not include visible personal or financial information. IT agents have access to users' screens for legitimate purposes and must exercise discretion. Capturing and storing a screenshot with personal banking data visible is a privacy violation.

prompt: An employee contacts the helpdesk and reports that her colleague has asked her for her login credentials to access a shared project file while she is at lunch. What should the helpdesk advise her to do?
options: Share only the password, not the username
Share the credentials since it is just a temporary arrangement between colleagues
Do not share her credentials under any circumstances. The correct approach is to share the specific file through the company's approved file-sharing system with the colleague's own account
Report the request to her manager and let the manager decide
explanation: Employees must never share their login credentials with colleagues, even for convenience. The correct approach is to share access to specific files or folders through an approved system that allows each person to access content using their own account.

prompt: A fire evacuation drill reveals that a locked server room has several people inside who were not logged in the visitor register. The server room requires registration upon entry. What does this indicate?
options: The fire drill was not communicated to IT in advance
People are entering the server room without following the registration requirement â€” this is a physical access control failure that needs to be investigated and corrected immediately
The register is not mandatory during emergency drills
The server room staff were too busy to maintain the register
explanation: If a drill reveals unregistered occupants in a secured area, the access control process is not being followed. This must be investigated â€” if staff regularly skip registration, unauthorised entries may have gone undetected.

prompt: An HR officer scans signed employment contracts and stores them in a shared cloud folder labelled 'HR Docs â€” All Staff,' accessible to all 120 employees across the company. What did she do wrong?
options: She should have used a different file naming convention
She stored sensitive personal documents containing employment terms and signatures in a folder accessible to everyone in the company, rather than a restricted, access-controlled HR-only location
Scanned documents should always remain as paper originals
She stored contracts without encrypting them
explanation: Employment contracts are sensitive personal documents. They must only be accessible to authorised HR personnel and relevant managers â€” not all company staff. Unrestricted folder access violates both data protection principles and employee confidentiality.

prompt: An IT helpdesk agent receives a ticket requesting access to the disciplinary records folder for an employee who works in the legal team. The ticket does not specify why access is needed. What should the agent do?
options: Grant the access â€” legal team members often need sensitive records
Grant temporary access and review after one week
Contact the requester to understand the business reason for the access, verify it with the appropriate HR or legal authority, and only grant access if it is justified and properly approved
Escalate the ticket to a senior agent without investigating further
explanation: Access to disciplinary records is highly sensitive and must be granted only when there is a verified, legitimate business need. A ticket with no stated reason is insufficient. The agent must confirm the purpose and obtain proper authorisation before granting access.

prompt: An operations manager wants to grant a temporary worker access to the company's warehouse booking system. She asks IT to set up the account but does not specify an end date for the access. What should IT ask before creating the account?
options: What the temporary worker's preferred username should be
When the temporary worker's assignment ends so the account can be set with an automatic expiry date matching the end of the engagement
Whether the temporary worker has used a similar system before
Whether the manager wants the account to have admin rights
explanation: Temporary worker accounts must include an expiry date aligned to the end of the engagement. Without an end date, the account will remain active after the worker leaves, creating unnecessary access risk. Always set an appropriate expiry at the point of creation.

prompt: A security guard notices a person has been sitting in the building lobby for two hours claiming to be waiting for a meeting. The reception team has no record of any scheduled visitor for that person. What should the guard do?
options: Allow them to continue waiting â€” meetings run late
Politely approach the person, ask them to confirm who they are meeting, and verify with the relevant team. If no confirmed meeting exists, ask them to wait outside until the visit is confirmed
Ignore the situation unless the person moves towards a restricted area
Ask another team member to keep an eye on the person
explanation: An unregistered individual in a building lobby for an extended period is a physical security concern. They could be gathering information or waiting for an opportunity to access a restricted area. A polite but firm verification approach is appropriate.

prompt: An employee calls the IT helpdesk to say his account has been locked after too many incorrect password attempts, but he is certain he did not try to log in at that time. What should the helpdesk agent do?
options: Unlock the account and reset the password so the employee can get back in
Tell the employee his account was probably locked by mistake and unlock it
Treat this as a potential account compromise. Escalate to IT Security, investigate the failed login attempts before unlocking, and only restore access after ensuring the account is secure
Unlock the account and ask the employee to monitor for anything unusual
explanation: Failed login attempts that the legitimate user did not make are a sign that someone else is attempting to access the account. Simply unlocking restores access before establishing whether the account has been targeted. Investigate first, then restore access securely.

prompt: During an HR investigation, the investigating officer accidentally sends the draft investigation report â€” including witness statements â€” to the employee under investigation. What must the HR officer do?
options: Ask the employee to delete the email and not read it

Immediately notify the investigation panel and HR leadership, follow the data breach reporting process, seek legal advice on the impact on the investigation, and communicate clearly with all parties involved
Send a corrected email to the panel and hope the employee ignores what they received
Pause the investigation until the situation is legally assessed
explanation: Sharing witness statements with the subject of an investigation is a serious breach of process and confidentiality. It can compromise the investigation, expose witnesses to risk, and create legal liability. The incident must be escalated immediately to HR leadership and legal counsel.

prompt: An employee's job role changes and she moves from the marketing team to the finance team. Six months later, a review reveals she still has access to the marketing shared drive and CRM system. What should have happened when her role changed?
options: She should have informed IT herself when she changed roles

Access to systems associated with her previous role should have been revoked as part of a formal role-change process at the time of the move, with only finance-relevant access granted for the new role
Marketing access can remain active in case she is asked to support the team temporarily
The access should be reviewed at the next annual audit
explanation: Role changes must trigger an immediate access review. Old access must be revoked and new, role-appropriate access provisioned. Retaining access to previous systems is a data control failure â€” not a convenience to be reviewed annually.

prompt: An operations team member finds a printed shipping manifest containing client names, addresses, and order values on the photocopier. It has been there for over an hour with no one claiming it. What should she do?
options: Leave it in case the owner comes back
Leave it face down to hide the information
Take it to the team leader or security desk immediately and report that sensitive client data was found unattended on a shared photocopier
Shred it so no one else can see the information
explanation: Unattended sensitive documents should be reported, not left or independently destroyed. The owner may need the document, and the incident should be logged so the pattern of leaving sensitive items unattended can be addressed.

prompt: An IT helpdesk agent is asked to set up multi-factor authentication on an employee's account. The employee asks the agent to set it up so that the agent's own mobile number receives the authentication codes, saying it will be easier. What should the agent do?
options: Agree â€” it is more practical and the agent can send codes when needed
Set up a shared code delivery method that both the agent and employee can access
Decline. MFA must be registered to the account holder's own verified device â€” not to a third party's number. Set up MFA using the employee's own mobile number or authenticator app
Set it up on the agent's number temporarily and transfer it later
explanation: Registering MFA to a helpdesk agent's number means the agent can access the account without the employee's knowledge. This completely undermines the purpose of MFA and gives the agent unchecked access. MFA must always be registered to the account owner.

prompt: During a building security audit, it is found that the server room access log shows the same badge was used 42 times in one month, but the badge belongs to an employee who went on long-term sick leave at the start of that month. What does this indicate?
options: The badge reader is logging errors and the entries should be deleted
Someone has been using this employee's badge to access the server room while they were on sick leave â€” this is a serious security incident requiring immediate investigation
The sick employee may have given their badge to a trusted colleague
Access logs sometimes carry over from previous months and the entries are probably historical
explanation: An access badge being used by someone other than its registered holder is a serious physical security incident. The employee's access should have been suspended when they went on leave. This must be investigated as a matter of urgency.

prompt: An employee tells the helpdesk she accidentally approved an MFA prompt she should have declined â€” someone was trying to log into her account and she pressed approve before realising. What should she do first?
options: Change her password and continue working
Do nothing since the login attempt has now succeeded and changing the password will fix it
Report the incident to IT Security immediately and ask for her account to be reviewed and secured â€” an attacker may now have active access to her account
Ask a colleague to check her email inbox for anything suspicious
explanation: Accidentally approving an MFA prompt for an unauthorised login may have given an attacker access to the account. This is an active security incident requiring immediate IT Security involvement to contain and investigate the breach.

prompt: An HR team is rolling out a new people management system and imports all employee data â€” including performance ratings, disciplinary history, and salary â€” into a test environment shared with the software vendor for configuration. What should have been done differently?
options: The import should have been done by the vendor, not HR

Real employee personal data should not be used in a test environment shared with an external vendor. Anonymised or synthetic test data should be used instead, with the vendor's access covered by a signed data agreement
The test environment should have had stronger passwords
The import was acceptable since the vendor is bound by contract
explanation: Test environments used with third-party vendors must use anonymised or dummy data â€” not real employee records. Using real data exposes personal information to the vendor unnecessarily, and once data is shared outside secure controls, it is very difficult to contain.

prompt: A caller to the IT helpdesk says she is an employee's PA and asks for the employee's email to be set up to automatically forward all incoming messages to her own inbox so she can manage correspondence while the employee is travelling. What should the agent do?
options: Set up the forwarding rule â€” PAs routinely manage executive email
Set up forwarding only for emails marked as high priority
Decline to set up automatic email forwarding without a formal, documented request from the account holder themselves, verified through the proper authorisation process
Set up the forwarding for one week only and review after that
explanation: Automatically forwarding all of someone's email to a third party â€” even their PA â€” must be authorised by the account holder through a formal process. Doing it on a PA's request alone creates a significant privacy and data control risk.

prompt: An IT agent is resolving a ticket for an employee and notices the employee's files include a folder named 'job applications' containing CVs submitted to other companies, saved on the work laptop. The agent says nothing. Did the agent do the right thing?
options: Yes â€” it is none of the agent's business what personal files are on the laptop
No â€” the agent should have flagged the personal files to the employee and reminded them that personal data stored on company laptops may be subject to IT review and violates acceptable-use policy
Yes â€” personal files on work laptops are always acceptable
No â€” the agent should have deleted the personal files immediately
explanation: Company laptops are subject to monitoring and review by IT. Employees should be made aware when personal data is found on work devices and reminded of the acceptable-use policy. The agent should not silently ignore it.

prompt: During an onboarding meeting, a new employee is given a laminated card with the warehouse Wi-Fi password on it to keep at their workstation. The card is also visible to visitors being toured through the warehouse. What is wrong with this?
options: The laminated card will not last long in a warehouse environment
Displaying a network password visibly in an area accessible to visitors means anyone touring the facility can read and use the company's network without authorisation
The card should have been issued by IT, not operations
A laminated card cannot be updated when the password changes
explanation: Network passwords must never be displayed in areas accessible to visitors or non-authorised users. Any visitor who reads the card can connect to the company's network. Passwords should be shared through secure channels and changed regularly.

prompt: An IT helpdesk agent notices that the same employee has raised four password reset tickets in one month. What should the agent do beyond simply processing the latest reset?
options: Process the reset and note that the employee is forgetful
Refuse the reset until the employee can explain why they keep forgetting

Process the reset but flag the pattern to a senior IT Security colleague, as repeated resets may indicate the employee is being targeted, has a compromised account, or is sharing their credentials with others
Suggest the employee write their password down in a safe place
explanation: Frequent password resets can be a warning sign of credential sharing, account targeting, or ongoing compromise attempts. The helpdesk should note patterns and escalate to IT Security â€” not simply process each ticket in isolation.

prompt: An operations team leader is asked to approve overtime submissions for her team members. She notices one team member has submitted overtime for a weekend shift that she is certain did not happen. What should she do?
options: Approve it to avoid conflict â€” small overtime amounts are not worth disputing
Decline the overtime claim and ask the employee for supporting evidence such as shift records or clock-in data before approving or rejecting
Approve it this time and monitor more closely going forward
Speak to the employee informally and ask them to withdraw the claim
explanation: Approving overtime that the manager believes did not occur is a financial control failure. The correct response is to request supporting evidence before making a decision â€” not to approve without verification.

prompt: A caller to IT support says she has just spilled coffee on her laptop and needs a replacement immediately. She gives her name but cannot provide her employee ID or any other verification details. What should the helpdesk agent do?
options: Issue a replacement immediately since she has given her name
Ask her to come to the IT desk in person so the team can verify her identity before issuing a replacement device
Ask a colleague to vouch for her over the phone before issuing the replacement
Issue the replacement and note that verification was not completed due to urgency
explanation: Issuing a replacement device to an unverified caller risks handing company equipment to someone who is not entitled to it. Asking the person to attend in person allows physical ID verification â€” this is entirely reasonable even in urgent situations.

prompt: An HR officer discovers that a reference check form for a job candidate contains the candidate's national insurance number, submitted by mistake, and the form has been seen by three members of the hiring panel. What should the HR officer do?
options: Delete the form and reissue it without the national insurance number
Immediately inform the candidate that their sensitive data was inadvertently included in a shared document, notify the hiring panel to destroy their copies, and report it as a data incident
Ask the hiring panel to delete the form from their email without reading it further
File it securely and take no further action since only staff have seen it
explanation: A national insurance number is sensitive personal data. Its inadvertent disclosure to multiple people must be handled as a data incident â€” the candidate must be informed, all copies secured or destroyed, and the incident logged through proper channels.

prompt: An employee working the night shift notices an unfamiliar laptop plugged into an Ethernet port in the server room corridor. No one is nearby. What should she do?
options: Unplug the laptop and put it in the lost and found box
Leave it â€” it probably belongs to an IT engineer working late

Do not touch the device but immediately alert the security team and IT Security so they can investigate, and treat the situation as a potential unauthorised network connection until confirmed otherwise
Photograph the device and report it to her manager in the morning
explanation: An unknown device connected to the corporate network in a sensitive area is a serious security incident. Do not touch or remove it â€” this could interfere with investigation. Alert security and IT Security immediately so they can assess whether an unauthorised connection has been made.

prompt: An operations manager collects all the access badges from her team at the end of a project and keeps them in her desk drawer rather than returning them to the security desk for deactivation. What is the risk?
options: The badges may be damaged in the drawer
The badges remain active in her possession and could be used by anyone who accesses her desk â€” they must be returned to security immediately for deactivation and proper logging
The badges should have been kept in a lockable safe, not a drawer
This is an acceptable temporary measure if the manager intends to return them soon
explanation: Access badges must be deactivated through the security desk â€” not stored by a manager. Active badges in a desk drawer could be taken and used to access secure areas. The physical return and deactivation process also ensures the asset register is updated.

prompt: An IT helpdesk agent is setting up a new employee's account and asks the employee's manager to choose a username and initial password, emailing both to the manager when done. What is wrong with this process?
options: The manager should not be involved in IT account setup
The initial password was emailed to the manager rather than the employee, meaning the manager knows the employee's starting credentials before the employee does â€” this should never happen
Usernames should not be chosen by managers
Account setup emails should be encrypted before sending
explanation: Account credentials â€” even temporary ones â€” should be sent only to the account holder. Sending them to a manager first gives the manager knowledge of the employee's starting password, which is a privacy violation and undermines individual account security from day one.

prompt: An HR team runs a company-wide survey asking employees to include their name alongside their answers, saying responses are confidential. Two weeks later, individual responses are visible to line managers. What went wrong?
options: The survey was too long and personal

The survey collected identifying information while claiming confidentiality, but the system allowed managers to view individual responses â€” the promise of confidentiality was broken and employees may have been misled
Employees should not have included their names
The results should have been shared only with senior leadership
explanation: If a survey is presented as confidential, the system must genuinely prevent identifiable responses from being seen by those in authority over respondents. Collecting names and then allowing managers to view them is a breach of the confidentiality promise and undermines trust.

prompt: An operations centre security officer reviews CCTV footage from a weekend for personal interest during a quiet shift, without any specific incident to investigate. What is wrong with this?
options: Weekend footage is not stored at high enough resolution to be useful
Reviewing CCTV footage without a legitimate business reason is an unjustified use of surveillance data, potentially violating the privacy rights of those recorded
CCTV should only be reviewed by senior security managers
The officer should have logged the review in the security system
explanation: CCTV footage is personal data collected for specific security purposes. Accessing it out of personal curiosity â€” without an incident to investigate â€” is an unauthorised use of surveillance data. It may breach data protection law and workplace privacy policies.

prompt: A caller to the IT helpdesk says she works in the London office but her email shows she is based in Edinburgh. She needs her password reset but does not know the answer to her security question. What should the helpdesk agent do?
options: Reset it anyway since the caller knows she is in the wrong location in the system
Ask an alternative question and reset if she gets it right
Decline to reset the password without successful completion of the standard identity verification process, and advise the caller to attend in person for identity verification
Ask the caller to email her manager to vouch for her before resetting
explanation: If a caller cannot pass the standard identity verification, the password must not be reset. Location discrepancies add further reason for caution. The correct path is to direct the caller to an in-person verification process rather than finding workarounds.

prompt: An employee in operations receives a call from a number he does not recognise. The caller claims to be from the company's IT team and asks the employee to read out the code displayed on his work laptop screen. The employee has not requested any IT support. What should he do?
options: Read out the code â€” IT staff need it for remote maintenance
Ask the caller for their employee ID before reading out the code
Do not read out the code. Hang up and call the IT helpdesk directly on the official number to report the call and check whether any genuine support action was initiated
Read out only part of the code to test if the caller is legitimate
explanation: Unsolicited calls asking for codes displayed on your screen are a social engineering technique to gain remote access. The legitimate IT helpdesk does not call employees out of the blue and ask for screen codes. Hang up and call IT directly to verify.

prompt: A new joiner in the HR team is given access to the entire HR database on her first day, including all salary data, medical information, and disciplinary records. Her role is to manage recruitment administration only. What should have happened instead?
options: She should have been given access gradually over her first month
Access should have been limited to only the systems and data relevant to recruitment administration â€” broad access to sensitive HR data beyond her role creates unnecessary risk
She should have signed an NDA before receiving any access
Full access is standard for new HR team members to help them understand the business
explanation: Access must be tailored to each individual's role requirements. Granting full HR database access to someone whose role only requires recruitment administration means she has visibility of sensitive data â€” salary, medical, disciplinary â€” that is entirely unnecessary for her work.

prompt: A senior manager asks the IT team to set up a hidden folder on the company network that only he and one other director can see, containing strategic plans. He asks IT not to document it in the system. What should IT do?
options: Set it up as requested â€” senior managers are entitled to private folders
Set up the folder but document it internally without telling the manager

Decline to create undocumented folders. All system configurations must be properly documented, and folders containing company data must comply with normal governance. Escalate to the IT director if the manager insists
Create the folder with a temporary name and wait for further instructions
explanation: Undocumented, hidden folders on the company network bypass governance, audit, and data management controls. No employee â€” regardless of seniority â€” can instruct IT to create infrastructure that is intentionally hidden from standard oversight processes.

prompt: An operations worker notices her colleague is regularly clocking in on behalf of another team member who arrives late. Both employees have asked her not to say anything. What should she do?
options: Stay silent â€” it is not her responsibility and she does not want conflict
Tell the team leader informally without naming the employees
Report the buddy-clocking behaviour through the appropriate channel â€” such as her supervisor or the HR team â€” as it is a falsification of attendance records and a breach of company policy
Clock in late herself occasionally to balance things out
explanation: Clocking in on behalf of another employee is a falsification of attendance records. It is dishonest, unfair to other employees, and may result in overpayment for hours not worked. It must be reported, even if it creates personal discomfort.

prompt: An IT helpdesk team has a policy that all calls must be logged as tickets. A senior IT staff member regularly resolves issues verbally over the phone without logging a ticket, saying it is faster. What is the problem?
options: Unlogged calls make it harder to calculate workload statistics

Unlogged resolutions create no audit trail, cannot be reviewed for quality or security, and mean patterns of issues â€” including potential security incidents â€” may be missed because they are never recorded
The helpdesk software is too slow to log every small call
Senior staff are experienced enough that logging is optional for them
explanation: Every helpdesk interaction must be logged regardless of seniority. Unlogged actions cannot be audited, reviewed for security concerns, or used to identify systemic issues. Patterns like repeated password resets for the same user are only visible if all interactions are recorded.

prompt: An employee in operations discovers that her work email password has been saved to the browser on a shared workstation used by multiple shift workers. What should she do?
options: Leave it â€” it is only accessible to colleagues on the same shift
Delete the saved password from the browser immediately, change her email password, and remind all shift workers that personal credentials must never be saved to shared devices
Ask her shift manager to remind everyone not to look at her emails
Report it to IT so they can delete all saved passwords from the browser
explanation: Saved credentials on a shared workstation mean any user of that device can access your account. Remove the saved password immediately, change the password, and ensure colleagues understand the risk of saving credentials on shared devices.

prompt: An HR assistant is leaving the office at the end of the day and realises her desk drawer â€” which contains signed employee contracts â€” is unlocked. She is in a hurry and plans to lock it first thing tomorrow. What should she do instead?
options: Leave it â€” the building is locked overnight so no one can access it
Ask a colleague to lock it before they leave
Lock the drawer before leaving. Building security does not eliminate the need for individual document security â€” cleaning staff, security guards, and others have building access overnight
Put the documents on top of her desk so she does not forget to secure them in the morning
explanation: Even in a locked building, multiple people have overnight access â€” including cleaners, security staff, and maintenance workers. Sensitive documents must always be secured before leaving, regardless of how secure the building itself appears.

prompt: A new IT support policy requires all helpdesk calls to be answered within three rings, putting pressure on agents to respond quickly. An agent answers a call and immediately resets a password without going through the verification steps because the queue is long. What did the agent do wrong?
options: He answered the call too quickly
He allowed time pressure from the response target to compromise the identity verification process, which must be completed regardless of call queue length or response time targets
He should have put the caller on hold while he verified their identity
He reset the password before confirming the ticket was raised correctly
explanation: Response time targets must never override security procedures. A fast answer time is a customer service metric; identity verification is a security control. An agent who skips verification to meet a call-time target creates a serious security risk.

prompt: An HR manager receives a call from someone claiming to be a former employee asking for a copy of their own employment record. The caller refuses to submit the request in writing and insists on an immediate verbal response. What should the HR manager do?
options: Read out the employment record details over the phone since the caller claims to be the former employee
Provide only the start and end dates since those are not sensitive
Explain that requests for personal records must be submitted in writing with proof of identity, and provide the correct process for making a Subject Access Request
Ask a colleague to verify the caller's voice before providing any information
explanation: Personal records cannot be shared over the phone with an unverified caller. A written Subject Access Request with identity verification is the correct and legally compliant route for anyone requesting their own data.

prompt: During a helpdesk shift, an agent notices that a colleague is logging in to closed tickets and changing their resolution notes. The colleague says she is just tidying up her notes. What should the agent do?
options: Leave it â€” tidying notes is harmless
Mention it to the colleague and ask her to stop
Report the behaviour to the IT Security or helpdesk manager, as editing closed tickets without a documented reason may be an attempt to alter the audit trail
Close the colleague's session remotely to prevent further changes
explanation: Closed helpdesk tickets form part of the audit trail. Editing them without a transparent, documented reason â€” especially habitually â€” raises concerns about what is being concealed. This must be reported so it can be investigated.

prompt: An operations supervisor is asked to participate in a third-party vendor audit. The auditor asks for a walkthrough of the warehouse and wants to photograph storage areas. What should the supervisor do before allowing photographs?
options: Allow all photos since the auditor has a legitimate audit purpose
Allow photos only of areas without staff present
Confirm with the compliance or legal team whether the audit scope permits photography, and ensure sensitive operational or client information is not visible in any shots before agreeing
Ask the auditor to email her the photos they want before taking them
explanation: Photography during a third-party audit must be within the agreed scope and must not inadvertently capture sensitive operational data, client details, or staff. Legal or compliance should confirm what is permissible before any photographs are taken.

prompt: An employee is on annual leave and a colleague notices the absent employee's computer is logged in and unlocked at their desk. What should the colleague do?
options: Lock the computer by pressing the keyboard shortcut on their behalf
Leave it â€” the employee will return shortly
Lock the screen on the employee's behalf, report the situation to the line manager, and remind the team of the importance of locking workstations before leaving
Log out fully to secure the account
